### Frozen SFR retrieved pool

<details><summary>Rank 1 · 19d5de0ab045f18f3c652f9a9af04a94 · document 1907.06292 · score 0.62844 · 256 tokens</summary>

<pre>to guide the workers. As for the answers, since the context we consider is relatively shorter than the context of previous datasets, we do not restrict the answers to be in the tweet, otherwise, the task may potentially be simplified as a classification problem. The workers are allowed to write their answers in their own words. We just require the answers to be brief and can be directly inferred from the tweets. After we retrieve the QA pairs from all HITs, we conduct further post-filtering to filter out the pairs from workers that obviously do not follow instructions. We remove QA pairs with yes/no answers. Questions with less than five words are also filtered out. This process filtered INLINEFORM0 of the QA pairs. The dataset now includes 10,898 articles, 17,794 tweets, and 13,757 crowdsourced question-answer pairs. The collected QA pairs will be directly available to the public, and we will provide a script to download the original tweets and detailed documentation on how we build our dataset. Also note that since we keep the original news article and news titles for each tweet, our dataset can also be used to explore more challenging generation tasks. Table TABREF19 shows the statistics of our current collection, and the</pre>

</details>

<details><summary>Rank 2 · 1c7acdf644ff85f056bf3303803bbff9 · document 1907.06292 · score 0.61004 · 256 tokens</summary>

<pre>large-scale dataset for QA over social media data. Rather than naively obtaining tweets from Twitter using the Twitter API which can yield irrelevant tweets with no valuable information, we restrict ourselves only to tweets which have been used by journalists in news articles thus implicitly implying that such tweets contain useful and relevant information. To obtain such relevant tweets, we crawled thousands of news articles that include tweet quotations and then employed crowd-sourcing to elicit questions and answers based on these event-aligned tweets. Table TABREF3 gives an example from our TweetQA dataset. It shows that QA over tweets raises challenges not only because of the informal nature of oral-style texts (e.g. inferring the answer from multiple short sentences, like the phrase “so young” that forms an independent sentence in the example), but also from tweet-specific expressions (such as inferring that it is “Jay Sean” feeling sad about Paul&#x27;s death because he posted the tweet). Furthermore, we show the distinctive nature of TweetQA by comparing the collected data with traditional QA datasets collected primarily from formal domains. In particular, we demonstrate empirically that three strong neural models which achieve good performance on formal data do not generalize well to social media data, bringing out challenges to developing QA systems that work well on social media domains. In summary,</pre>

</details>

<details><summary>Rank 3 · 65c7fe2301726db3cb15d5a0ee2a72d2 · document 1907.06292 · score 0.58027 · 255 tokens</summary>

<pre>them are partially equivalent (one of them is incomplete) and INLINEFORM4 are totally inconsistent. The answers collected at this step are also used to measure the human performance. We have 59 individual workers participated in this process.

Task and Evaluation	As described in the question-answer writing process, the answers in our dataset are different from those in some existing extractive datasets. Thus we consider the task of answer generation for TweetQA and we use several standard metrics for natural language generation to evaluate QA systems on our dataset, namely we consider BLEU-1  , Meteor  and Rouge-L  in this paper. To evaluate machine systems, we compute the scores using both the original answer and validation answer as references. For human performance, we use the validation answers as generated ones and the original answers as references to calculate the scores.

Analysis	In this section, we analyze our dataset and outline the key properties that distinguish it from standard QA datasets like SQuAD  . First, our dataset is derived from social media text which can be quite informal and user-centric as opposed to SQuAD which is derived from Wikipedia and hence more formal in nature. We observe that the shared vocabulary between SQuAD and TweetQA is only INLINEFORM0 , suggesting a significant difference in their lexical</pre>

</details>

<details><summary>Rank 4 · 36fe361a9cb26b54f5ba248619fb67b6 · document 1907.06292 · score 0.57899 · 256 tokens</summary>

<pre>the tweets that are posted by the official Twitter accounts of news media. However, these tweets are often just the summaries of news articles, which are written in formal text. As our focus is to develop a dataset for QA on informal social media text, we do not consider this approach. After we extracted tweets from archived news articles, we observed that there is still a portion of tweets that have very simple semantic structures and thus are very difficult to raise meaningful questions. An example of such tweets can be like: “Wanted to share this today - @IAmSteveHarvey&quot;. This tweet is actually talking about an image attached to this tweet. Some other tweets with simple text structures may talk about an inserted link or even videos. To filter out these tweets that heavily rely on attached media to convey information, we utilize a state-of-the-art semantic role labeling model trained on CoNLL-2005  to analyze the predicate-argument structure of the tweets collected from news articles and keep only the tweets with more than two labeled arguments. This filtering process also automatically filters out most of the short tweets. For the tweets collected from CNN, INLINEFORM0 of them were filtered via semantic role labeling. For tweets from NBC, INLINEFORM1 of the tweets were filtered. We</pre>

</details>

<details><summary>Rank 5 · 0c2f68854c9dc30c25908755bae7399e · document 1907.06292 · score 0.57274 · 156 tokens</summary>

<pre>entities to choose from, which could make the answer pattern easy to learn. On the other hand, the neural models fail to perform well on the “Why” questions, and the results of neural baselines are even worse than that of the matching baseline. We find that these questions generally have longer answer phrases than other types of questions, with the average answer length being 3.74 compared to 2.13 for any other types. Also, since all the answers are written by humans instead of just spans from the context, these abstractive answers can make it even harder for current models to handle. We also observe that when people write “Why” questions, they tend to copy word spans from the tweet, potentially making the task easier for the matching baseline.</pre>

</details>

<details><summary>Rank 6 · d84ae9be8767f3cb50ce7944025971d2 · document 1907.06292 · score 0.56342 · 256 tokens</summary>

<pre>content. Figure FIGREF25 shows the 1000 most distinctive words in each domain as extracted from SQuAD and TweetQA. Note the stark differences in the words seen in the TweetQA dataset, which include a large number of user accounts with a heavy tail. Examples include @realdonaldtrump, @jdsutter, @justinkirkland and #cnnworldcup, #goldenglobes. In contrast, the SQuAD dataset rarely has usernames or hashtags that are used to signify events or refer to the authors. It is also worth noting that the data collected from social media can not only capture events and developments in real-time but also capture individual opinions and thus requires reasoning related to the authorship of the content as is illustrated in Table TABREF3 . In addition, while SQuAD requires all answers to be spans from the given passage, we do not enforce any such restriction and answers can be free-form text. In fact, we observed that INLINEFORM1 of our QA pairs consists of answers which do not have an exact substring matching with their corresponding passages. All of the above distinguishing factors have implications to existing models which we analyze in upcoming sections. We conduct analysis on a subset of TweetQA to get a better understanding</pre>

</details>

<details><summary>Rank 7 · 61f5c0e831b5ff7fdc88664b2ee19928 · document 1907.06292 · score 0.56301 · 256 tokens</summary>

<pre>our contributions are:

TweetQA	In this section, we first describe the three-step data collection process of TweetQA: tweet crawling, question-answer writing and answer validation. Next, we define the specific task of TweetQA and discuss several evaluation metrics. To better understand the characteristics of the TweetQA task, we also include our analysis on the answer and question characteristics using a subset of QA pairs from the development set.

Data Collection	One major challenge of building a QA dataset on tweets is the sparsity of informative tweets. Many users write tweets to express their feelings or emotions about their personal lives. These tweets are generally uninformative and also very difficult to ask questions about. Given the linguistic variance of tweets, it is generally hard to directly distinguish those tweets from informative ones. In terms of this, rather than starting from Twitter API Search, we look into the archived snapshots of two major news websites (CNN, NBC), and then extract the tweet blocks that are embedded in the news articles. In order to get enough data, we first extract the URLs of all section pages (e.g. World, Politics, Money, Tech) from the snapshot of each home page and then crawl all articles with tweets from these section pages. <details><summary>Rank 8 · fe8bc1cb7a7f9b312c3c3b2ccffd0980 · document 1907.06292 · score 0.56287 · 256 tokens</summary>

<pre>TWEETQA: A Social Media Focused Question Answering Dataset	With social media becoming increasingly pop-ular on which lots of news and real-time eventsare reported, developing automated questionanswering systems is critical to the effective-ness of many applications that rely on real-time knowledge. While previous datasets haveconcentrated on question answering (QA) forformal text like news and Wikipedia, wepresent the first large-scale dataset for QA oversocial media data. To ensure that the tweetswe collected are useful, we only gather tweetsused by journalists to write news articles. Wethen ask human annotators to write questionsand answers upon these tweets. Unlike otherQA datasets like SQuAD in which the answersare extractive, we allow the answers to be ab-stractive. We show that two recently proposedneural models that perform well on formaltexts are limited in their performance when ap-plied to our dataset. In addition, even the fine-tuned BERT model is still lagging behind hu-man performance with a large margin. Our re-sults thus point to the need of improved QAsystems targeting social media text.

Introduction	Social media is now becoming an important real-time information source, especially during natural disasters and emergencies. It is now very</pre>

</details>

<pre>frequency of different types of questions is shown in Table TABREF21 . All QA pairs were written by 492 individual workers. For the purposes of human performance evaluation and inter-annotator agreement checking, we launch a different set of HITs to ask workers to answer questions in the test and development set. The workers are shown with the tweet blocks as well as the questions collected in the previous step. At this step, workers are allowed to label the questions as “NA&quot; if they think the questions are not answerable. We find that INLINEFORM0 of the questions are labeled as unanswerable by the workers (for SQuAD, the ratio is INLINEFORM1 ). Since the answers collected at this step and previous step are written by different workers, the answers can be written in different text forms even they are semantically equal to each other. For example, one answer can be “Hillary Clinton” while the other is “@HillaryClinton”. As it is not straightforward to automatically calculate the overall agreement, we manually check the agreement on a subset of 200 random samples from the development set and ask an independent human moderator to verify the result. It turns out that INLINEFORM2 of the answers pairs are semantically equivalent, INLINEFORM3 of</pre>

<details><summary>Rank 10 · 9e5ddc0f1548e5659cc5fc8beb69f37d · document 1907.06292 · score 0.56112 · 256 tokens</summary>

<pre>then use Amazon Mechanical Turk to collect question-answer pairs for the filtered tweets. For each Human Intelligence Task (HIT), we ask the worker to read three tweets and write two question-answer pairs for each tweet. To ensure the quality, we require the workers to be located in major English speaking countries (i.e. Canada, US, and UK) and have an acceptance rate larger than INLINEFORM0 . Since we use tweets as context, lots of important information are contained in hashtags or even emojis. Instead of only showing the text to the workers, we use javascript to directly embed the whole tweet into each HIT. This gives workers the same experience as reading tweets via web browsers and help them to better compose questions. To avoid trivial questions that can be simply answered by superficial text matching methods or too challenging questions that require background knowledge. We explicitly state the following items in the HIT instructions for question writing: No Yes-no questions should be asked. The question should have at least five words. Videos, images or inserted links should not be considered. No background knowledge should be required to answer the question. To help the workers better follow the instructions, we also include a representative example showing both good and bad questions or answers in our instructions. Figure FIGREF14 shows the example we use</pre>

#### What V1 discarded / V2 recovered

<pre>{
  &quot;FIXED_SENTENCE_sentences_absent_in_V1&quot;: [
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;2c4828d63e86a7c5710110baf81ffdc6&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;65c7fe2301726db3cb15d5a0ee2a72d2&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Analysis\tIn this section, we analyze our dataset and outline the key properties that distinguish it from standard QA datasets like SQuAD  .&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;35d6097d8c423de91449b7018ba8793f&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;fe8bc1cb7a7f9b312c3c3b2ccffd0980&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;While previous datasets haveconcentrated on question answering (QA) forformal text like news and Wikipedia, wepresent the first large-scale dataset for QA oversocial media data.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;7894229a221788c018eec749cbee4f56&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;19d5de0ab045f18f3c652f9a9af04a94&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;The dataset now includes 10,898 articles, 17,794 tweets, and 13,757 crowdsourced question-answer pairs.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;84fb58321653fb2863805af4ff81f64d&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;19d5de0ab045f18f3c652f9a9af04a94&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;The collected QA pairs will be directly available to the public, and we will provide a script to download the original tweets and detailed documentation on how we build our dataset.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;b2d14903325470e808fa21ce64b9d5f8&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;65c7fe2301726db3cb15d5a0ee2a72d2&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;First, our dataset is derived from social media text which can be quite informal and user-centric as opposed to SQuAD which is derived from Wikipedia and hence more formal in nature.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;babbf261c88eb1ad4db0eae5b3f6cfa2&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;d84ae9be8767f3cb50ce7944025971d2&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Note the stark differences in the words seen in the TweetQA dataset, which include a large number of user accounts with a heavy tail.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;c54a0880f3d13de2dbceb73d4ee2c3ec&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;19d5de0ab045f18f3c652f9a9af04a94&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Also note that since we keep the original news article and news titles for each tweet, our dataset can also be used to explore more challenging generation tasks.&quot;
    }
  ],
  &quot;QBGF_FULL_sentences_absent_in_V1&quot;: [
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;0bf839a0d3a28b1cef4f70de95f6e2fb&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;1c7acdf644ff85f056bf3303803bbff9&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Furthermore, we show the distinctive nature of TweetQA by comparing the collected data with traditional QA datasets collected primarily from formal domains.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;213ca270649f67c17ccd9c76507ce55d&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;1c7acdf644ff85f056bf3303803bbff9&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;To obtain such relevant tweets, we crawled thousands of news articles that include tweet quotations and then employed crowd-sourcing to elicit questions and answers based on these event-aligned tweets.&quot;
    },

We observe some correlation between these numbers and accuracy on the main task: for de, en, ru and sv, the brown, pink and blue bars here pattern in the same way as the corresponding INLINEFORM0 &#x27;s in Figure FIGREF23 . One notable exception to this pattern is fr where inflection gains a lot from multilingual training, while MSD prediction suffers greatly. Notice that the magnitude of change is not always the same, however, even when the general direction matches: for ru, for example, multilingual training benefits inflection much more than in benefits MSD prediction, even though the MSD decoder is the only component that is actually shared between languages. This observation illustrates the two-fold effect of multi-task training: an auxiliary task can either inform the main task through the parameters the two tasks share, or it can help the main task learning through its regularising effect.

<pre>the models are indeed being finetuned rather than retrained. We keep all hyperparameters the same as in the baseline. Training data is split 90:10 for training and validation. We train our models for 50 epochs, adding early stopping with a tolerance of five epochs of no improvement in the validation loss. We do not subsample from the training data. We train models for 50 different random combinations of two to three languages in Track 1, and 50 monolingual models for each language in Track 2. Instead of picking the single model that performs best on the development set and thus risking to select a model that highly overfits that data, we use an ensemble of the five best models, and make the final prediction for a given target form with a majority vote over the five predictions.

Results and Discussion	Test results are listed in Table TABREF17 . Our system outperforms the baseline for all settings and languages in Track 1 and for almost all in Track 2—only in the high resource setting is our system not definitively superior to the baseline. Interestingly, our results in the low resource setting are often higher for Track 2 than for Track 1, even though contextual information is less explicit in the</pre>

<pre>de, en, fr, ru and sv. For the other two languages in the dataset, es and fi, the difference between this approach and the approach that emerged as best for them is less than 1%. The overall improvement of the multilingual multi-tasking approach over the baseline is 18.30%.

Error analysis	Here we study the errors produced by our system on the English test set to better understand the remaining shortcomings of the approach. A small portion of the wrong predictions point to an incorrect interpretation of the morpho-syntactic conditioning of the context, e.g. the system predicted plan instead of plans in the context Our _ include raising private capital. The majority of wrong predictions, however, are nonsensical, like bomb for job, fify for fixing, and gnderrate for understand. This observation suggests that generally the system did not learn to copy the characters of lemma into inflected form, which is all it needs to do in a large number of cases. This issue could be alleviated with simple data augmentation techniques that encourage autoencoding  .

Multi-task learning, paired with multilingual training and subsequent monolingual finetuning, scored highest for five out of seven languages, improving accuracy by another 9.86% on average.

Our system	Here we compare and contrast our system to the baseline system. A diagram of our system is shown in Figure FIGREF4 . The idea behind this modification is to provide the encoder with access to all morpho-syntactic cues present in the sentence. In contrast to the baseline, which only encodes the immediately adjacent context of a target word, we encode the entire context. All context word forms, lemmas, and MSD tags (in Track 1) are embedded in their respective high-dimensional spaces as before, and their embeddings are concatenated. However, we now reduce the entire past context to a fixed-size vector by encoding it with a forward LSTM, and we similarly represent the future context by encoding it with a backwards LSTM. We introduce an auxiliary objective that is meant to increase the morpho-syntactic awareness of the encoder and to regularise the learning process—the task is to predict the MSD tag of the target form. ### Frozen SFR retrieved pool

<details><summary>Rank 1 · 19d5de0ab045f18f3c652f9a9af04a94 · document 1907.06292 · score 0.62844 · 256 tokens</summary>

<pre>to guide the workers. As for the answers, since the context we consider is relatively shorter than the context of previous datasets, we do not restrict the answers to be in the tweet, otherwise, the task may potentially be simplified as a classification problem. The workers are allowed to write their answers in their own words. We just require the answers to be brief and can be directly inferred from the tweets. After we retrieve the QA pairs from all HITs, we conduct further post-filtering to filter out the pairs from workers that obviously do not follow instructions. We remove QA pairs with yes/no answers. Questions with less than five words are also filtered out. This process filtered INLINEFORM0 of the QA pairs. The dataset now includes 10,898 articles, 17,794 tweets, and 13,757 crowdsourced question-answer pairs. The collected QA pairs will be directly available to the public, and we will provide a script to download the original tweets and detailed documentation on how we build our dataset. Also note that since we keep the original news article and news titles for each tweet, our dataset can also be used to explore more challenging generation tasks. Table TABREF19 shows the statistics of our current collection, and the</pre>

</details>

<details><summary>Rank 2 · 1c7acdf644ff85f056bf3303803bbff9 · document 1907.06292 · score 0.61004 · 256 tokens</summary>

<pre>large-scale dataset for QA over social media data. Rather than naively obtaining tweets from Twitter using the Twitter API which can yield irrelevant tweets with no valuable information, we restrict ourselves only to tweets which have been used by journalists in news articles thus implicitly implying that such tweets contain useful and relevant information. To obtain such relevant tweets, we crawled thousands of news articles that include tweet quotations and then employed crowd-sourcing to elicit questions and answers based on these event-aligned tweets. Table TABREF3 gives an example from our TweetQA dataset. It shows that QA over tweets raises challenges not only because of the informal nature of oral-style texts (e.g. inferring the answer from multiple short sentences, like the phrase “so young” that forms an independent sentence in the example), but also from tweet-specific expressions (such as inferring that it is “Jay Sean” feeling sad about Paul&#x27;s death because he posted the tweet). Furthermore, we show the distinctive nature of TweetQA by comparing the collected data with traditional QA datasets collected primarily from formal domains. In particular, we demonstrate empirically that three strong neural models which achieve good performance on formal data do not generalize well to social media data, bringing out challenges to developing QA systems that work well on social media domains. In summary,</pre>

</details>

<details><summary>Rank 3 · 65c7fe2301726db3cb15d5a0ee2a72d2 · document 1907.06292 · score 0.58027 · 255 tokens</summary>

<pre>them are partially equivalent (one of them is incomplete) and INLINEFORM4 are totally inconsistent. The answers collected at this step are also used to measure the human performance. We have 59 individual workers participated in this process.

Task and Evaluation	As described in the question-answer writing process, the answers in our dataset are different from those in some existing extractive datasets. Thus we consider the task of answer generation for TweetQA and we use several standard metrics for natural language generation to evaluate QA systems on our dataset, namely we consider BLEU-1  , Meteor  and Rouge-L  in this paper. To evaluate machine systems, we compute the scores using both the original answer and validation answer as references. For human performance, we use the validation answers as generated ones and the original answers as references to calculate the scores.

Analysis	In this section, we analyze our dataset and outline the key properties that distinguish it from standard QA datasets like SQuAD  . First, our dataset is derived from social media text which can be quite informal and user-centric as opposed to SQuAD which is derived from Wikipedia and hence more formal in nature. We observe that the shared vocabulary between SQuAD and TweetQA is only INLINEFORM0 , suggesting a significant difference in their lexical</pre>

</details>

<details><summary>Rank 4 · 36fe361a9cb26b54f5ba248619fb67b6 · document 1907.06292 · score 0.57899 · 256 tokens</summary>

<pre>the tweets that are posted by the official Twitter accounts of news media. However, these tweets are often just the summaries of news articles, which are written in formal text. As our focus is to develop a dataset for QA on informal social media text, we do not consider this approach. TweetQA	In this section, we first describe the three-step data collection process of TweetQA: tweet crawling, question-answer writing and answer validation. Next, we define the specific task of TweetQA and discuss several evaluation metrics. To better understand the characteristics of the TweetQA task, we also include our analysis on the answer and question characteristics using a subset of QA pairs from the development set.

Data Collection	One major challenge of building a QA dataset on tweets is the sparsity of informative tweets. Many users write tweets to express their feelings or emotions about their personal lives. These tweets are generally uninformative and also very difficult to ask questions about. Given the linguistic variance of tweets, it is generally hard to directly distinguish those tweets from informative ones. In terms of this, rather than starting from Twitter API Search, we look into the archived snapshots of two major news websites (CNN, NBC), and then extract the tweet blocks that are embedded in the news articles. In order to get enough data, we first extract the URLs of all section pages (e.g. World, Politics, Money, Tech) from the snapshot of each home page and then crawl all articles with tweets from these section pages. <pre>TWEETQA: A Social Media Focused Question Answering Dataset	With social media becoming increasingly pop-ular on which lots of news and real-time eventsare reported, developing automated questionanswering systems is critical to the effective-ness of many applications that rely on real-time knowledge. While previous datasets haveconcentrated on question answering (QA) forformal text like news and Wikipedia, wepresent the first large-scale dataset for QA oversocial media data. To ensure that the tweetswe collected are useful, we only gather tweetsused by journalists to write news articles. Wethen ask human annotators to write questionsand answers upon these tweets. Unlike otherQA datasets like SQuAD in which the answersare extractive, we allow the answers to be ab-stractive. We show that two recently proposedneural models that perform well on formaltexts are limited in their performance when ap-plied to our dataset. In addition, even the fine-tuned BERT model is still lagging behind hu-man performance with a large margin. Our re-sults thus point to the need of improved QAsystems targeting social media text.

TweetQA	In this section, we first describe the three-step data collection process of TweetQA: tweet crawling, question-answer writing and answer validation.

To better understand the characteristics of the TweetQA task, we also include our analysis on the answer and question characteristics using a subset of QA pairs from the development set.

Data Collection	One major challenge of building a QA dataset on tweets is the sparsity of informative tweets.

In terms of this, rather than starting from Twitter API Search, we look into the archived snapshots of two major news websites (CNN, NBC), and then extract the tweet blocks that are embedded in the news articles.

In order to get enough data, we first extract the URLs of all section pages (e.g. World, Politics, Money, Tech) from the snapshot of each home page and then crawl all articles with tweets from these section pages.

To filter out these tweets that heavily rely on attached media to convey information, we utilize a state-of-the-art semantic role labeling model trained on CoNLL-2005  to analyze the predicate-argument structure of the tweets collected from news articles and keep only the tweets with more than two labeled arguments.

then use Amazon Mechanical Turk to collect question-answer pairs for the filtered tweets.

As for the answers, since the context we consider is relatively shorter than the context of previous datasets, we do not restrict the answers to be in the tweet, otherwise, the task may potentially be simplified as a classification problem.

The dataset now includes 10,898 articles, 17,794 tweets, and 13,757 crowdsourced question-answer pairs.

The collected QA pairs will be directly available to the public, and we will provide a script to download the original tweets and detailed documentation on how we build our dataset.

Also note that since we keep the original news article and news titles for each tweet, our dataset can also be used to explore more challenging generation tasks.

Task and Evaluation	As described in the question-answer writing process, the answers in our dataset are different from those in some existing extractive datasets.

Thus we consider the task of answer generation for TweetQA and we use several standard metrics for natural language generation to evaluate QA systems on our dataset, namely we consider BLEU-1  , Meteor  and Rouge-L  in this paper.

      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;61f5c0e831b5ff7fdc88664b2ee19928&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1907.06292&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 3974,
      &quot;end&quot;: 3996,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 4,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;our contributions are:&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;609d627fc035ea9ab5e86339dc5c5808&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;61f5c0e831b5ff7fdc88664b2ee19928&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1907.06292&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 3998,
      &quot;end&quot;: 4154,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 29,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;TweetQA\tIn this section, we first describe the three-step data collection process of TweetQA: tweet crawling, question-answer writing and answer validation.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;277eee24ce0f93e984e2352a18c0e7ff&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;61f5c0e831b5ff7fdc88664b2ee19928&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1907.06292&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 4240,
      &quot;end&quot;: 4426,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 33,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;To better understand the characteristics of the TweetQA task, we also include our analysis on the answer and question characteristics using a subset of QA pairs from the development set.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;8705804e5df344e021b441f0a4c4e00b&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;61f5c0e831b5ff7fdc88664b2ee19928&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1907.06292&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 4428,
      &quot;end&quot;: 4537,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 21,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Data Collection\tOne major challenge of building a QA dataset on tweets is the sparsity of informative tweets.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;1f82cd9955e7f96e2588631e6f2bfe81&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;61f5c0e831b5ff7fdc88664b2ee19928&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1907.06292&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 4839,
      &quot;end&quot;: 5051,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 43,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;In terms of this, rather than starting from Twitter API Search, we look into the archived snapshots of two major news websites (CNN, NBC), and then extract the tweet blocks that are embedded in the news articles.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;78947a43449e1cadea70f5ba1d65689a&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;61f5c0e831b5ff7fdc88664b2ee19928&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1907.06292&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 5052,
      &quot;end&quot;: 5265,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 47,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;In order to get enough data, we first extract the URLs of all section pages (e.g. World, Politics, Money, Tech) from the snapshot of each home page and then crawl all articles with tweets from these section pages.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;82640ee9edff088b742bc1c8fed45517&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;36fe361a9cb26b54f5ba248619fb67b6&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1907.06292&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 6088,
      &quot;end&quot;: 6405,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 63,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;To filter out these tweets that heavily rely on attached media to convey information, we utilize a state-of-the-art semantic role labeling model trained on CoNLL-2005  to analyze the predicate-argument structure of the tweets collected from news articles and keep only the tweets with more than two labeled arguments.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;2face8fc71b6857827c85ac89e1cfd8c&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;9e5ddc0f1548e5659cc5fc8beb69f37d&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1907.06292&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 6648,
      &quot;end&quot;: 6737,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 15,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;then use Amazon Mechanical Turk to collect question-answer pairs for the filtered tweets.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;0b86376d936a39c9ce6a782447d63fd8&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;19d5de0ab045f18f3c652f9a9af04a94&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1907.06292&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 8057,
      &quot;end&quot;: 8297,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 45,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;As for the answers, since the context we consider is relatively shorter than the context of previous datasets, we do not restrict the answers to be in the tweet, otherwise, the task may potentially be simplified as a classification problem.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;7894229a221788c018eec749cbee4f56&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;19d5de0ab045f18f3c652f9a9af04a94&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1907.06292&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 8761,
      &quot;end&quot;: 8864,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 36,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;The dataset now includes 10,898 articles, 17,794 tweets, and 13,757 crowdsourced question-answer pairs.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;84fb58321653fb2863805af4ff81f64d&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;19d5de0ab045f18f3c652f9a9af04a94&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1907.06292&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 8865,
      &quot;end&quot;: 9046,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 33,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;The collected QA pairs will be directly available to the public, and we will provide a script to download the original tweets and detailed documentation on how we build our dataset.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;c54a0880f3d13de2dbceb73d4ee2c3ec&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;19d5de0ab045f18f3c652f9a9af04a94&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1907.06292&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 9047,
      &quot;end&quot;: 9208,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 30,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Also note that since we keep the original news article and news titles for each tweet, our dataset can also be used to explore more challenging generation tasks.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;2d60a2c1e341242c260c47259ba02a02&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;19d5de0ab045f18f3c652f9a9af04a94&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1907.06292&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 9209,
      &quot;end&quot;: 9279,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 15,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Table TABREF19 shows the statistics of our current collection, and the&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;8817edad496feec0e844c06611c196be&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;86d47a772276fb3430305ee64c766e73&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1907.06292&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 9280,
      &quot;end&quot;: 9350,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 15,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;frequency of different types of questions is shown in Table TABREF21 .&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;cb843e6b4fa3d81f003981a62c713979&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;86d47a772276fb3430305ee64c766e73&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1907.06292&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 9404,
      &quot;end&quot;: 9594,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 36,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;For the purposes of human performance evaluation and inter-annotator agreement checking, we launch a different set of HITs to ask workers to answer questions in the test and development set.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;fa986892dcd18facd346b7898b0e1990&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;86d47a772276fb3430305ee64c766e73&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1907.06292&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 9809,
      &quot;end&quot;: 9933,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 31,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;We find that INLINEFORM0 of the questions are labeled as unanswerable by the workers (for SQuAD, the ratio is INLINEFORM1 ).&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;c323c43297b61f019d090222d2fcbeb8&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;65c7fe2301726db3cb15d5a0ee2a72d2&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1907.06292&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 10539,
      &quot;end&quot;: 10638,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 19,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;them are partially equivalent (one of them is incomplete) and INLINEFORM4 are totally inconsistent.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;24ca07c70695a43206391eec3414c92c&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;65c7fe2301726db3cb15d5a0ee2a72d2&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1907.06292&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 10783,
      &quot;end&quot;: 10945,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 29,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Task and Evaluation\tAs described in the question-answer writing process, the answers in our dataset are different from those in some existing extractive datasets.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;a4e91e27c8af13ad3bdb5fd383851fb7&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;65c7fe2301726db3cb15d5a0ee2a72d2&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1907.06292&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 10946,
      &quot;end&quot;: 11176,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 48,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Thus we consider the task of answer generation for TweetQA and we use several standard metrics for natural language generation to evaluate QA systems on our dataset, namely we consider BLEU-1  , Meteor  and Rouge-L  in this paper.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;2c4828d63e86a7c5710110baf81ffdc6&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;65c7fe2301726db3cb15d5a0ee2a72d2&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1907.06292&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 11432,
      &quot;end&quot;: 11571,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 27,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Analysis\tIn this section, we analyze our dataset and outline the key properties that distinguish it from standard QA datasets like SQuAD  .&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;b2d14903325470e808fa21ce64b9d5f8&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;65c7fe2301726db3cb15d5a0ee2a72d2&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1907.06292&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 11572,
      &quot;end&quot;: 11754,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 36,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;First, our dataset is derived from social media text which can be quite informal and user-centric as opposed to SQuAD which is derived from Wikipedia and hence more formal in nature.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;f8a64563907e63affddb1695b0fe5039&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;d84ae9be8767f3cb50ce7944025971d2&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1907.06292&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 11903,
      &quot;end&quot;: 12008,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 28,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Figure FIGREF25 shows the 1000 most distinctive words in each domain as extracted from SQuAD and TweetQA.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;babbf261c88eb1ad4db0eae5b3f6cfa2&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;d84ae9be8767f3cb50ce7944025971d2&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1907.06292&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 12009,
      &quot;end&quot;: 12142,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 27,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Note the stark differences in the words seen in the TweetQA dataset, which include a large number of user accounts with a heavy tail.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;650d364fe4b06ed833e95be0f055ce7d&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;d84ae9be8767f3cb50ce7944025971d2&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1907.06292&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 12238,
      &quot;end&quot;: 12358,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 25,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;In contrast, the SQuAD dataset rarely has usernames or hashtags that are used to signify events or refer to the authors.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;1876aeec9624e81bcbf8e9c3272224a2&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;d84ae9be8767f3cb50ce7944025971d2&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1907.06292&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 12359,
      &quot;end&quot;: 12625,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 48,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;It is also worth noting that the data collected from social media can not only capture events and developments in real-time but also capture individual opinions and thus requires reasoning related to the authorship of the content as is illustrated in Table TABREF3 .&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;e3b04a4ffc762fea670c1403e7ddca04&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;0c2f68854c9dc30c25908755bae7399e&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1907.06292&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 23996,
      &quot;end&quot;: 24172,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 39,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;We find that these questions generally have longer answer phrases than other types of questions, with the average answer length being 3.74 compared to 2.13 for any other types.&quot;
    }

<pre>{
  &quot;selected_units&quot;: [

      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;While previous datasets haveconcentrated on question answering (QA) forformal text like news and Wikipedia, wepresent the first large-scale dataset for QA oversocial media data.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;c45e2e2fce8b570b75efea12a0cc3374&quot;,

      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Furthermore, we show the distinctive nature of TweetQA by comparing the collected data with traditional QA datasets collected primarily from formal domains.&quot;

      &quot;tokens&quot;: 256,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;the tweets that are posted by the official Twitter accounts of news media. However, these tweets are often just the summaries of news articles, which are written in formal text. As our focus is to develop a dataset for QA on informal social media text, we do not consider this approach. After we extracted tweets from archived news articles, we observed that there is still a portion of tweets that have very simple semantic structures and thus are very difficult to raise meaningful questions. An example of such tweets can be like: “Wanted to share this today - @IAmSteveHarvey\&quot;. This tweet is actually talking about an image attached to this tweet. Some other tweets with simple text structures may talk about an inserted link or even videos. To filter out these tweets that heavily rely on attached media to convey information, we utilize a state-of-the-art semantic role labeling model trained on CoNLL-2005  to analyze the predicate-argument structure of the tweets collected from news articles and keep only the tweets with more than two labeled arguments. This filtering process also automatically filters out most of the short tweets. For the tweets collected from CNN, INLINEFORM0 of them were filtered via semantic role labeling. For tweets from NBC, INLINEFORM1 of the tweets were filtered. We&quot;

      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;For each Human Intelligence Task (HIT), we ask the worker to read three tweets and write two question-answer pairs for each tweet.&quot;

    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;19d5de0ab045f18f3c652f9a9af04a94&quot;,

      &quot;end&quot;: 9279,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 256,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;to guide the workers. As for the answers, since the context we consider is relatively shorter than the context of previous datasets, we do not restrict the answers to be in the tweet, otherwise, the task may potentially be simplified as a classification problem. The workers are allowed to write their answers in their own words. We just require the answers to be brief and can be directly inferred from the tweets. After we retrieve the QA pairs from all HITs, we conduct further post-filtering to filter out the pairs from workers that obviously do not follow instructions. We remove QA pairs with yes/no answers. Questions with less than five words are also filtered out. This process filtered INLINEFORM0 of the QA pairs. The dataset now includes 10,898 articles, 17,794 tweets, and 13,757 crowdsourced question-answer pairs. The collected QA pairs will be directly available to the public, and we will provide a script to download the original tweets and detailed documentation on how we build our dataset. Also note that since we keep the original news article and news titles for each tweet, our dataset can also be used to explore more challenging generation tasks. Table TABREF19 shows the statistics of our current collection, and the&quot;

      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 4240,
      &quot;end&quot;: 4426,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 33,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;To better understand the characteristics of the TweetQA task, we also include our analysis on the answer and question characteristics using a subset of QA pairs from the development set.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;8705804e5df344e021b441f0a4c4e00b&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;61f5c0e831b5ff7fdc88664b2ee19928&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1907.06292&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 4428,
      &quot;end&quot;: 4537,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 21,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Data Collection\tOne major challenge of building a QA dataset on tweets is the sparsity of informative tweets.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;78947a43449e1cadea70f5ba1d65689a&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;61f5c0e831b5ff7fdc88664b2ee19928&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1907.06292&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 5052,
      &quot;end&quot;: 5265,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 47,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;In order to get enough data, we first extract the URLs of all section pages (e.g. World, Politics, Money, Tech) from the snapshot of each home page and then crawl all articles with tweets from these section pages.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;2b8745dba59302d3c35ef41d873f9c57&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;36fe361a9cb26b54f5ba248619fb67b6&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1907.06292&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 5520,
      &quot;end&quot;: 5628,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 23,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;As our focus is to develop a dataset for QA on informal social media text, we do not consider this approach.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;65db1751c03b1db53f668c57a4cab583&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;36fe361a9cb26b54f5ba248619fb67b6&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1907.06292&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 5924,
      &quot;end&quot;: 5993,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 13,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;This tweet is actually talking about an image attached to this tweet.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;03229ab15b6fc93f9f1bf66c7af91df5&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;36fe361a9cb26b54f5ba248619fb67b6&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1907.06292&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 6406,
      &quot;end&quot;: 6485,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 13,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;This filtering process also automatically filters out most of the short tweets.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;42eb74ac80a62c738282c6129f990d38&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;36fe361a9cb26b54f5ba248619fb67b6&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1907.06292&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 6486,
      &quot;end&quot;: 6582,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 19,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;For the tweets collected from CNN, INLINEFORM0 of them were filtered via semantic role labeling.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;2face8fc71b6857827c85ac89e1cfd8c&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;9e5ddc0f1548e5659cc5fc8beb69f37d&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1907.06292&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 6648,
      &quot;end&quot;: 6737,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 15,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;then use Amazon Mechanical Turk to collect question-answer pairs for the filtered tweets.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;8574e8712b7ebe8bd48ef4bd5fc4645a&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;9e5ddc0f1548e5659cc5fc8beb69f37d&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1907.06292&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 6738,
      &quot;end&quot;: 6868,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 27,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;For each Human Intelligence Task (HIT), we ask the worker to read three tweets and write two question-answer pairs for each tweet.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;5ad272cd8336ad333b117ce30a6a965a&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;9e5ddc0f1548e5659cc5fc8beb69f37d&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1907.06292&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 6869,
      &quot;end&quot;: 7044,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 39,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;To ensure the quality, we require the workers to be located in major English speaking countries (i.e. Canada, US, and UK) and have an acceptance rate larger than INLINEFORM0 .&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;613ba0e14c7a1e38fe3c48c21acb7d93&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;9e5ddc0f1548e5659cc5fc8beb69f37d&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1907.06292&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 7045,
      &quot;end&quot;: 7148,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 19,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Since we use tweets as context, lots of important information are contained in hashtags or even emojis.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;2a6603b9c7962bb12dc7e97eee9c0811&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;9e5ddc0f1548e5659cc5fc8beb69f37d&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1907.06292&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 7149,
      &quot;end&quot;: 7264,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 23,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Instead of only showing the text to the workers, we use javascript to directly embed the whole tweet into each HIT.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;c37e7817903de332769b76cc6bc5ad46&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;9e5ddc0f1548e5659cc5fc8beb69f37d&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1907.06292&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 7538,
      &quot;end&quot;: 7660,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 22,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;We explicitly state the following items in the HIT instructions for question writing: No Yes-no questions should be asked.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;81e877bfa21927b2fa351374a07d7db9&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;9e5ddc0f1548e5659cc5fc8beb69f37d&quot;,

      &quot;start&quot;: 7661,
      &quot;end&quot;: 7706,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 9,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;The question should have at least five words.&quot;
    },

      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;9e5ddc0f1548e5659cc5fc8beb69f37d&quot;,

      &quot;start&quot;: 8761,
      &quot;end&quot;: 8864,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 36,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;The dataset now includes 10,898 articles, 17,794 tweets, and 13,757 crowdsourced question-answer pairs.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;84fb58321653fb2863805af4ff81f64d&quot;,

      &quot;start&quot;: 8865,
      &quot;end&quot;: 9046,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 33,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;The collected QA pairs will be directly available to the public, and we will provide a script to download the original tweets and detailed documentation on how we build our dataset.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;c54a0880f3d13de2dbceb73d4ee2c3ec&quot;,

      &quot;start&quot;: 9047,
      &quot;end&quot;: 9208,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 30,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Also note that since we keep the original news article and news titles for each tweet, our dataset can also be used to explore more challenging generation tasks.&quot;
    },
    {

      &quot;end&quot;: 9403,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 13,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;All QA pairs were written by 492 individual workers.&quot;
    },
    {

      &quot;end&quot;: 9933,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 31,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;We find that INLINEFORM0 of the questions are labeled as unanswerable by the workers (for SQuAD, the ratio is INLINEFORM1 ).&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;cb4e2580651323d182687a1b6434edfa&quot;,

      &quot;start&quot;: 10213,
      &quot;end&quot;: 10443,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 42,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;As it is not straightforward to automatically calculate the overall agreement, we manually check the agreement on a subset of 200 random samples from the development set and ask an independent human moderator to verify the result.&quot;
    },
    {

      &quot;end&quot;: 10638,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 19,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;them are partially equivalent (one of them is incomplete) and INLINEFORM4 are totally inconsistent.&quot;
    },
    {

      &quot;tokens&quot;: 15,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;The answers collected at this step are also used to measure the human performance.&quot;
    },

      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;We have 59 individual workers participated in this process.&quot;

      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;65c7fe2301726db3cb15d5a0ee2a72d2&quot;,

      &quot;end&quot;: 10945,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 29,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Task and Evaluation\tAs described in the question-answer writing process, the answers in our dataset are different from those in some existing extractive datasets.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;a4e91e27c8af13ad3bdb5fd383851fb7&quot;,

      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1907.06292&quot;,

      &quot;start&quot;: 10946,
      &quot;end&quot;: 11176,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 48,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Thus we consider the task of answer generation for TweetQA and we use several standard metrics for natural language generation to evaluate QA systems on our dataset, namely we consider BLEU-1  , Meteor  and Rouge-L  in this paper.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;6477fb43b42f63e855ff3dca622fa1f4&quot;,

      &quot;start&quot;: 11177,
      &quot;end&quot;: 11295,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 20,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;To evaluate machine systems, we compute the scores using both the original answer and validation answer as references.&quot;
    },

      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;2c4828d63e86a7c5710110baf81ffdc6&quot;,

      &quot;start&quot;: 11432,
      &quot;end&quot;: 11571,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 27,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Analysis\tIn this section, we analyze our dataset and outline the key properties that distinguish it from standard QA datasets like SQuAD  .&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;b2d14903325470e808fa21ce64b9d5f8&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;65c7fe2301726db3cb15d5a0ee2a72d2&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1907.06292&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 11572,
      &quot;end&quot;: 11754,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 36,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;First, our dataset is derived from social media text which can be quite informal and user-centric as opposed to SQuAD which is derived from Wikipedia and hence more formal in nature.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;f8a64563907e63affddb1695b0fe5039&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;d84ae9be8767f3cb50ce7944025971d2&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1907.06292&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 11903,
      &quot;end&quot;: 12008,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 28,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Figure FIGREF25 shows the 1000 most distinctive words in each domain as extracted from SQuAD and TweetQA.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;babbf261c88eb1ad4db0eae5b3f6cfa2&quot;,

      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1907.06292&quot;,

      &quot;end&quot;: 12142,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 27,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Note the stark differences in the words seen in the TweetQA dataset, which include a large number of user accounts with a heavy tail.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;650d364fe4b06ed833e95be0f055ce7d&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;d84ae9be8767f3cb50ce7944025971d2&quot;,

      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;In contrast, the SQuAD dataset rarely has usernames or hashtags that are used to signify events or refer to the authors.&quot;

#### What V1 discarded / V2 recovered

<pre>{
  &quot;FIXED_SENTENCE_sentences_absent_in_V1&quot;: [
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;0b86376d936a39c9ce6a782447d63fd8&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;19d5de0ab045f18f3c652f9a9af04a94&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;As for the answers, since the context we consider is relatively shorter than the context of previous datasets, we do not restrict the answers to be in the tweet, otherwise, the task may potentially be simplified as a classification problem.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;0bf839a0d3a28b1cef4f70de95f6e2fb&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;1c7acdf644ff85f056bf3303803bbff9&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Furthermore, we show the distinctive nature of TweetQA by comparing the collected data with traditional QA datasets collected primarily from formal domains.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;1876aeec9624e81bcbf8e9c3272224a2&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;d84ae9be8767f3cb50ce7944025971d2&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;It is also worth noting that the data collected from social media can not only capture events and developments in real-time but also capture individual opinions and thus requires reasoning related to the authorship of the content as is illustrated in Table TABREF3 .&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;1f82cd9955e7f96e2588631e6f2bfe81&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;61f5c0e831b5ff7fdc88664b2ee19928&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;In terms of this, rather than starting from Twitter API Search, we look into the archived snapshots of two major news websites (CNN, NBC), and then extract the tweet blocks that are embedded in the news articles.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;24ca07c70695a43206391eec3414c92c&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;65c7fe2301726db3cb15d5a0ee2a72d2&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Task and Evaluation\tAs described in the question-answer writing process, the answers in our dataset are different from those in some existing extractive datasets.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;277eee24ce0f93e984e2352a18c0e7ff&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;61f5c0e831b5ff7fdc88664b2ee19928&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;To better understand the characteristics of the TweetQA task, we also include our analysis on the answer and question characteristics using a subset of QA pairs from the development set.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;2c4828d63e86a7c5710110baf81ffdc6&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;65c7fe2301726db3cb15d5a0ee2a72d2&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Analysis\tIn this section, we analyze our dataset and outline the key properties that distinguish it from standard QA datasets like SQuAD  .&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;35d6097d8c423de91449b7018ba8793f&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;fe8bc1cb7a7f9b312c3c3b2ccffd0980&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;While previous datasets haveconcentrated on question answering (QA) forformal text like news and Wikipedia, wepresent the first large-scale dataset for QA oversocial media data.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;609d627fc035ea9ab5e86339dc5c5808&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;61f5c0e831b5ff7fdc88664b2ee19928&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;TweetQA\tIn this section, we first describe the three-step data collection process of TweetQA: tweet crawling, question-answer writing and answer validation.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;650d364fe4b06ed833e95be0f055ce7d&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;d84ae9be8767f3cb50ce7944025971d2&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;In contrast, the SQuAD dataset rarely has usernames or hashtags that are used to signify events or refer to the authors.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;7894229a221788c018eec749cbee4f56&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;19d5de0ab045f18f3c652f9a9af04a94&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;The dataset now includes 10,898 articles, 17,794 tweets, and 13,757 crowdsourced question-answer pairs.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;78947a43449e1cadea70f5ba1d65689a&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;61f5c0e831b5ff7fdc88664b2ee19928&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;In order to get enough data, we first extract the URLs of all section pages (e.g. World, Politics, Money, Tech) from the snapshot of each home page and then crawl all articles with tweets from these section pages.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;82640ee9edff088b742bc1c8fed45517&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;36fe361a9cb26b54f5ba248619fb67b6&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;To filter out these tweets that heavily rely on attached media to convey information, we utilize a state-of-the-art semantic role labeling model trained on CoNLL-2005  to analyze the predicate-argument structure of the tweets collected from news articles and keep only the tweets with more than two labeled arguments.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;84fb58321653fb2863805af4ff81f64d&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;19d5de0ab045f18f3c652f9a9af04a94&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;The collected QA pairs will be directly available to the public, and we will provide a script to download the original tweets and detailed documentation on how we build our dataset.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;8705804e5df344e021b441f0a4c4e00b&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;61f5c0e831b5ff7fdc88664b2ee19928&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Data Collection\tOne major challenge of building a QA dataset on tweets is the sparsity of informative tweets.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;99b19d402d072b662b62daa6f0bdba41&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;fe8bc1cb7a7f9b312c3c3b2ccffd0980&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;TWEETQA: A Social Media Focused Question Answering Dataset\tWith social media becoming increasingly pop-ular on which lots of news and real-time eventsare reported, developing automated questionanswering systems is critical to the effective-ness of many applications that rely on real-time knowledge.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;a035c95d11d5fe4c0fb731802d52349d&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;fe8bc1cb7a7f9b312c3c3b2ccffd0980&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Unlike otherQA datasets like SQuAD in which the answersare extractive, we allow the answers to be ab-stractive.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;a4e91e27c8af13ad3bdb5fd383851fb7&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;65c7fe2301726db3cb15d5a0ee2a72d2&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Thus we consider the task of answer generation for TweetQA and we use several standard metrics for natural language generation to evaluate QA systems on our dataset, namely we consider BLEU-1  , Meteor  and Rouge-L  in this paper.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;b2d14903325470e808fa21ce64b9d5f8&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;65c7fe2301726db3cb15d5a0ee2a72d2&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;First, our dataset is derived from social media text which can be quite informal and user-centric as opposed to SQuAD which is derived from Wikipedia and hence more formal in nature.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;babbf261c88eb1ad4db0eae5b3f6cfa2&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;d84ae9be8767f3cb50ce7944025971d2&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Note the stark differences in the words seen in the TweetQA dataset, which include a large number of user accounts with a heavy tail.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;c323c43297b61f019d090222d2fcbeb8&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;65c7fe2301726db3cb15d5a0ee2a72d2&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;them are partially equivalent (one of them is incomplete) and INLINEFORM4 are totally inconsistent.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;c45e2e2fce8b570b75efea12a0cc3374&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;fe8bc1cb7a7f9b312c3c3b2ccffd0980&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;We show that two recently proposedneural models that perform well on formaltexts are limited in their performance when ap-plied to our dataset.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;c54a0880f3d13de2dbceb73d4ee2c3ec&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;19d5de0ab045f18f3c652f9a9af04a94&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Also note that since we keep the original news article and news titles for each tweet, our dataset can also be used to explore more challenging generation tasks.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;cb843e6b4fa3d81f003981a62c713979&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;86d47a772276fb3430305ee64c766e73&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;For the purposes of human performance evaluation and inter-annotator agreement checking, we launch a different set of HITs to ask workers to answer questions in the test and development set.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;e3b04a4ffc762fea670c1403e7ddca04&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;0c2f68854c9dc30c25908755bae7399e&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;We find that these questions generally have longer answer phrases than other types of questions, with the average answer length being 3.74 compared to 2.13 for any other types.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;f8a64563907e63affddb1695b0fe5039&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;d84ae9be8767f3cb50ce7944025971d2&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Figure FIGREF25 shows the 1000 most distinctive words in each domain as extracted from SQuAD and TweetQA.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;fa986892dcd18facd346b7898b0e1990&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;86d47a772276fb3430305ee64c766e73&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;We find that INLINEFORM0 of the questions are labeled as unanswerable by the workers (for SQuAD, the ratio is INLINEFORM1 ).&quot;
    }
  ],
  &quot;QBGF_FULL_sentences_absent_in_V1&quot;: [
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;03229ab15b6fc93f9f1bf66c7af91df5&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;36fe361a9cb26b54f5ba248619fb67b6&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;This filtering process also automatically filters out most of the short tweets.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;047b4cbf383eb4ff0bb7ada252d8db12&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;36fe361a9cb26b54f5ba248619fb67b6&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;An example of such tweets can be like: “Wanted to share this today - @IAmSteveHarvey\&quot;.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;0b86376d936a39c9ce6a782447d63fd8&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;19d5de0ab045f18f3c652f9a9af04a94&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;As for the answers, since the context we consider is relatively shorter than the context of previous datasets, we do not restrict the answers to be in the tweet, otherwise, the task may potentially be simplified as a classification problem.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;0bf839a0d3a28b1cef4f70de95f6e2fb&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;1c7acdf644ff85f056bf3303803bbff9&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Furthermore, we show the distinctive nature of TweetQA by comparing the collected data with traditional QA datasets collected primarily from formal domains.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;192c23610c68a77a1620dbf157b1b473&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;36fe361a9cb26b54f5ba248619fb67b6&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;After we extracted tweets from archived news articles, we observed that there is still a portion of tweets that have very simple semantic structures and thus are very difficult to raise meaningful questions.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;213ca270649f67c17ccd9c76507ce55d&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;1c7acdf644ff85f056bf3303803bbff9&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;To obtain such relevant tweets, we crawled thousands of news articles that include tweet quotations and then employed crowd-sourcing to elicit questions and answers based on these event-aligned tweets.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;24432aeee5741b4204ab2c1e2e19ec8d&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;19d5de0ab045f18f3c652f9a9af04a94&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;After we retrieve the QA pairs from all HITs, we conduct further post-filtering to filter out the pairs from workers that obviously do not follow instructions.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;2b8745dba59302d3c35ef41d873f9c57&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;36fe361a9cb26b54f5ba248619fb67b6&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;As our focus is to develop a dataset for QA on informal social media text, we do not consider this approach.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;2c4828d63e86a7c5710110baf81ffdc6&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;65c7fe2301726db3cb15d5a0ee2a72d2&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Analysis\tIn this section, we analyze our dataset and outline the key properties that distinguish it from standard QA datasets like SQuAD  .&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;30a0b3a481856d3f66f86c264591f488&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;36fe361a9cb26b54f5ba248619fb67b6&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;For tweets from NBC, INLINEFORM1 of the tweets were filtered.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;35d6097d8c423de91449b7018ba8793f&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;fe8bc1cb7a7f9b312c3c3b2ccffd0980&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;While previous datasets haveconcentrated on question answering (QA) forformal text like news and Wikipedia, wepresent the first large-scale dataset for QA oversocial media data.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;42eb74ac80a62c738282c6129f990d38&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;36fe361a9cb26b54f5ba248619fb67b6&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;For the tweets collected from CNN, INLINEFORM0 of them were filtered via semantic role labeling.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;7894229a221788c018eec749cbee4f56&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;19d5de0ab045f18f3c652f9a9af04a94&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;The dataset now includes 10,898 articles, 17,794 tweets, and 13,757 crowdsourced question-answer pairs.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;82640ee9edff088b742bc1c8fed45517&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;36fe361a9cb26b54f5ba248619fb67b6&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;To filter out these tweets that heavily rely on attached media to convey information, we utilize a state-of-the-art semantic role labeling model trained on CoNLL-2005  to analyze the predicate-argument structure of the tweets collected from news articles and keep only the tweets with more than two labeled arguments.&quot;
    },
    {

Training and hyperparameter selection	We performed two sets of experiments with the single-trial EEG data. In PHASE-ONE, our goals was to identify the best architectures and hyperparameters for our networks with a reasonable number of runs. For PHASE-ONE, we randomly shuffled and divided the data (1913 signals from 14 individuals) into train (80%), development (10%) and test sets (10%). In PHASE-TWO, in order to perform a fair comparison with the previous methods reported on the same dataset, we perform</pre>

<pre>22.59%  and 17.52%  to a mere 5.41%.

Conclusion and future direction	In an attempt to move a step towards understanding the speech information encoded in brain signals, we developed a novel mixed deep neural network scheme for a number of binary classification tasks from speech imagery EEG data. Unlike previous approaches which mostly deal with subject-dependent classification of EEG into discrete vowel or word labels, this work investigates a subject-invariant mapping of EEG data with different phonological categories, varying widely in terms of underlying articulator motions (eg: involvement or non-involvement of lips and velum, variation of tongue movements etc). Our model takes an advantage of feature extraction capability of CNN, LSTM as well as the deep learning benefit of deep autoencoders. We took  ,  as the baseline works investigating the same problem and compared our performance with theirs. Our proposed method highly outperforms the existing methods across all the five binary classification tasks by a large average margin of 22.51%.

<details><summary>Rank 7 · 931fdd1335a2fff620465dfa8af93937 · document 1904.04358 · score 0.64210 · 256 tokens</summary>

<pre>Deep Learning the EEG Manifold for Phonological Categorization from Active Thoughts	Speech-related Brain Computer Interfaces (BCI) aim primarily at finding an alternative vocal communication pathway for people with speaking disabilities. As a step towards full decoding of imagined speech from active thoughts, we present a BCI system for subject-independent classification of phonological categories exploiting a novel deep learning based hierarchical feature extraction scheme. To better capture the complex representation of high-dimensional electroencephalography (EEG) data, we compute the joint variability of EEG electrodes into a channel cross-covariance matrix. We then extract the spatio-temporal information encoded within the matrix using a mixed deep neural network strategy. Our model framework is composed of a convolutional neural network (CNN), a long-short term network (LSTM), and a deep autoencoder. We train the individual networks hierarchically, feeding their combined outputs in a final gradient boosting classification step. Our best models achieve an average accuracy of 77.9% across five different binary classification tasks, providing a significant 22.5% improvement over previous methods. As we also show visually, our work demonstrates that the speech imagery EEG possesses significant discriminative information about the intended articulatory movements responsible for natural speech synthesis.

Joint variability of electrodes	Multichannel EEG data is high dimensional multivariate time series data whose dimensionality depends on the number of electrodes. It is a major hurdle to optimally encode information from these EEG data into lower dimensional space.       &quot;text&quot;: &quot;To this end, we develop our mixed neural network architecture composed of three supervised and a single unsupervised learning step, discussed in the next subsections and shown in Fig. FIGREF1 .&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;6c89e5ff6c4ec452d089e5b8e602f878&quot;,
