      &quot;start&quot;: 6310,
      &quot;end&quot;: 6636,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 60,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;In fact, our investigation based on a development set (as we explain later) showed that well-known deep neural networks (e.g., fully connected networks such as convolutional neural networks, recurrent neural networks and autoencoders) fail to individually learn such complex feature representations from single-trial EEG data.&quot;
    },
    {

      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;8573e921c8d083b9e72cddde1c0c089c&quot;,

      &quot;tokens&quot;: 37,

      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Classification with Extreme Gradient Boost\tAt the third level of hierarchy, the discrete latent vector representation of the deep autoencoder is fed into an Extreme Gradient Boost based classification layer  ,  motivated by  .&quot;
    },

      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;The classifier receives its input from the latent vectors of the deep autoencoder and is trained in a supervised manner to output the final predicted classes corresponding to the speech imagery.&quot;

      &quot;tokens&quot;: 73,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Performance analysis and discussion\tTo demonstrate the significance of the hierarchical CNN-LSTM-DAE method, we conducted separate experiments with the individual networks in PHASE-ONE of experiments and summarized the results in Table TABREF12 From the average accuracy scores, we observe that the mixed network performs much better than individual blocks which is in agreement with the findings in  .&quot;

      &quot;end&quot;: 13412,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 23,

      &quot;end&quot;: 14162,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 40,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;It also proves that the combined supervised and unsupervised neural networks, trained hierarchically, can learn the discriminative manifold better than the individual networks and it is crucial for improving the classification accuracy.&quot;

      &quot;end&quot;: 15701,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 29,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Besides, our best model shows more reliability compared to previous works: The standard deviation of our model&#x27;s classification accuracy across all the tasks is reduced from&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;bc450068bb39f3b011e7d94a9c95bc33&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;ff7b903669b2158076fffc609421540e&quot;,

      &quot;start&quot;: 15740,
      &quot;end&quot;: 15999,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 43,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Conclusion and future direction\tIn an attempt to move a step towards understanding the speech information encoded in brain signals, we developed a novel mixed deep neural network scheme for a number of binary classification tasks from speech imagery EEG data.&quot;
    },

      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;ff7b903669b2158076fffc609421540e&quot;,

      &quot;tokens&quot;: 66,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Unlike previous approaches which mostly deal with subject-dependent classification of EEG into discrete vowel or word labels, this work investigates a subject-invariant mapping of EEG data with different phonological categories, varying widely in terms of underlying articulator motions (eg: involvement or non-involvement of lips and velum, variation of tongue movements etc).&quot;

#### What V1 discarded / V2 recovered

<pre>{
  &quot;FIXED_SENTENCE_sentences_absent_in_V1&quot;: [
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;0454970f969d3badeea83dc361777504&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;8f9789a76d7318ea31b41155fa62d246&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;To further investigate the feature representation achieved by our model, we plot T-distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (tSNE) corresponding to INLINEFORM0 and V/C classification tasks in Fig. FIGREF8 .&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;14e5c6d0baee25ecd2b498ebbd2aa7f7&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;8573e921c8d083b9e72cddde1c0c089c&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;encodings and cancel background noise effects  , we train an unsupervised deep autoenoder (DAE) on the fused heterogeneous features produced by the combined CNN and LSTM information.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;39d73f0f1aba7051844785d57471a27a&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;9e88003d1c67f6b7366159a104932f25&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;For the gradient boosting classification, we fixed the maximum depth at 10, number of estimators at 5000, learning rate at 0.1, regularization coefficient at 0.3, subsample ratio at 0.8, and column-sample/iteration at 0.4.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;3cf7f19535a11ef9d17b553e9538e5b8&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;2fefe5a05c80135a90534482603aea18&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;It also proves that the combined supervised and unsupervised neural networks, trained hierarchically, can learn the discriminative manifold better than the individual networks and it is crucial for improving the classification accuracy.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;4a25550fa1a85d132c251c69e46b4f43&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;651ceda52a02eaa90a35bfcb119bf3f2&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;This includes categorization of imagined EEG signal into binary vowel categories like /a/, /u/ and rest  ,  ,  ; binary syllable classes like /ba/ and /ku/  ,  ,  ,  ; a handful of control words like &#x27;up&#x27;, &#x27;down&#x27;, &#x27;left&#x27;, &#x27;right&#x27; and &#x27;select&#x27;  or others like &#x27;water&#x27;, &#x27;help&#x27;, &#x27;thanks&#x27;, &#x27;food&#x27;, &#x27;stop&#x27;  , Chinese characters  , etc. Such works mostly involve traditional signal processing or manual feature handcrafting along with linear classifiers (e.g., SVMs).&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;4babf3524e99624c3b361703917e986c&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;931fdd1335a2fff620465dfa8af93937&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Our best models achieve an average accuracy of 77.9% across five different binary classification tasks, providing a significant 22.5% improvement over previous methods.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;56c4d323532e489fda8a5f93f07367d2&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;b736fdb8ed6f45bf7f8ccd13ce4ec636&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;For PHASE-ONE, we randomly shuffled and divided the data (1913 signals from 14 individuals) into train (80%), development (10%) and test sets (10%).&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;57ab0afa2b13dfada1782380c463b0e0&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;8f9789a76d7318ea31b41155fa62d246&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Next, we provide performance comparison of the proposed approach with the baseline methods for PHASE-TWO of our study (cross-validation experiment) in Table TABREF15 .&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;6c89e5ff6c4ec452d089e5b8e602f878&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;09d1024c4fcf7be485a0172bb610af23&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;In fact, our investigation based on a development set (as we explain later) showed that well-known deep neural networks (e.g., fully connected networks such as convolutional neural networks, recurrent neural networks and autoencoders) fail to individually learn such complex feature representations from single-trial EEG data.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;83e3785c08478f6d5474d41ca34b9767&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;8573e921c8d083b9e72cddde1c0c089c&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;The classifier receives its input from the latent vectors of the deep autoencoder and is trained in a supervised manner to output the final predicted classes corresponding to the speech imagery.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;89dec5c880a37c7f44833d3ef0d0cfa0&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;b736fdb8ed6f45bf7f8ccd13ce4ec636&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;In order to explore the problem space, we thus specifically target five binary classification problems addressed in  ,  , i.e presence/absence of consonants, phonemic nasal, bilabial, high-front vowels and high-back vowels.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;a47cd0cfcde7c8d53bdf8b9392151579&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;8573e921c8d083b9e72cddde1c0c089c&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Classification with Extreme Gradient Boost\tAt the third level of hierarchy, the discrete latent vector representation of the deep autoencoder is fed into an Extreme Gradient Boost based classification layer  ,  motivated by  .&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;a6e1d1f949e523c7a6572b15111e5808&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;ff7b903669b2158076fffc609421540e&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Unlike previous approaches which mostly deal with subject-dependent classification of EEG into discrete vowel or word labels, this work investigates a subject-invariant mapping of EEG data with different phonological categories, varying widely in terms of underlying articulator motions (eg: involvement or non-involvement of lips and velum, variation of tongue movements etc).&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;bc450068bb39f3b011e7d94a9c95bc33&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;ff7b903669b2158076fffc609421540e&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Conclusion and future direction\tIn an attempt to move a step towards understanding the speech information encoded in brain signals, we developed a novel mixed deep neural network scheme for a number of binary classification tasks from speech imagery EEG data.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;c1465fd4beb2938182114c10bebd87c4&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;9e88003d1c67f6b7366159a104932f25&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Performance analysis and discussion\tTo demonstrate the significance of the hierarchical CNN-LSTM-DAE method, we conducted separate experiments with the individual networks in PHASE-ONE of experiments and summarized the results in Table TABREF12 From the average accuracy scores, we observe that the mixed network performs much better than individual blocks which is in agreement with the findings in  .&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;c7349d951035c80716fb380af31646ea&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;8f9789a76d7318ea31b41155fa62d246&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Besides, our best model shows more reliability compared to previous works: The standard deviation of our model&#x27;s classification accuracy across all the tasks is reduced from&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;dbd7a7c8de85f5b9268a9bd36c81589d&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;35f82bdfb3449d9fe69567632bfe1c4b&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;To this end, we develop our mixed neural network architecture composed of three supervised and a single unsupervised learning step, discussed in the next subsections and shown in Fig. FIGREF1 .&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;e490ca15b39fba394d713c4c3e0f2208&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;931fdd1335a2fff620465dfa8af93937&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;As a step towards full decoding of imagined speech from active thoughts, we present a BCI system for subject-independent classification of phonological categories exploiting a novel deep learning based hierarchical feature extraction scheme.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;ef9761e9703df9fab67810d2d56c708b&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;931fdd1335a2fff620465dfa8af93937&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Deep Learning the EEG Manifold for Phonological Categorization from Active Thoughts\tSpeech-related Brain Computer Interfaces (BCI) aim primarily at finding an alternative vocal communication pathway for people with speaking disabilities.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;fb27ac467d35a35e94a847b35d2f1881&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;35f82bdfb3449d9fe69567632bfe1c4b&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;In  , Zhao et al. used manually handcrafted features from EEG data, combined with speech audio and facial features to achieve classification of the phonological categories varying based on the articulatory steps.&quot;
    }
  ],
  &quot;QBGF_FULL_sentences_absent_in_V1&quot;: [
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;0454970f969d3badeea83dc361777504&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;8f9789a76d7318ea31b41155fa62d246&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;To further investigate the feature representation achieved by our model, we plot T-distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (tSNE) corresponding to INLINEFORM0 and V/C classification tasks in Fig. FIGREF8 .&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;14e5c6d0baee25ecd2b498ebbd2aa7f7&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;8573e921c8d083b9e72cddde1c0c089c&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;encodings and cancel background noise effects  , we train an unsupervised deep autoenoder (DAE) on the fused heterogeneous features produced by the combined CNN and LSTM information.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;1c2dcf3d283d883fef6d50c6a7605607&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;b736fdb8ed6f45bf7f8ccd13ce4ec636&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;In PHASE-TWO, in order to perform a fair comparison with the previous methods reported on the same dataset, we perform&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;2395ec4aa31b72d5302ca81116df7c6a&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;b736fdb8ed6f45bf7f8ccd13ce4ec636&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;The dataset consists of 14 participants, with each prompt presented 11 times to each individual.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;261f55f00f3510f0286a7910fdec6b10&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;b736fdb8ed6f45bf7f8ccd13ce4ec636&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;In PHASE-ONE, our goals was to identify the best architectures and hyperparameters for our networks with a reasonable number of runs.&quot;
    },
    {

<pre>learn our own word vectors from the training and validation sets with the gensim implementation of word2vec . MPAD was implemented in Python 3.6 using the PyTorch library . All experiments were run on a single machine consisting of a 3.4 GHz Intel Core i7 CPU with 16 GB of RAM and an NVidia GeForce Titan Xp GPU.

Results and ablations ::: Results	Experimental results are shown in Table TABREF28. For the baselines, the best scores reported in each original paper are shown. MPAD reaches best performance on 7 out of 10 datasets, and is close second elsewhere. Moreover, the 7 datasets on which MPAD ranks first widely differ in training set size, number of categories, and prediction task (topic, sentiment, subjectivity), which indicates that MPAD can perform well in different settings. MPAD vs. hierarchical variants. On 9 datasets out of 10, one or more of the hierarchical variants outperform the vanilla MPAD architecture, highlighting the benefit of explicitly modeling the hierarchical nature of documents. However, on Subjectivity, standard MPAD outperforms all hierarchical variants. On TREC, it reaches the same accuracy. We hypothesize that in some cases, using</pre>

</details>

<details><summary>Rank 3 · fe21f767a06eb1c4d9d92bbcdfc014ae · document 1908.06267 · score 0.55394 · 256 tokens</summary>

<pre>a different graph to separately encode each sentence might be worse than using one single graph to directly encode the document. Indeed, in the single document graph, some words that never appear in the same sentence can be connected through common neighbors, as was explained in subsection SECREF7. So, this way, some notion of cross-sentence context is captured while learning representations of words, bigrams, etc. at each MP iteration. This creates better informed representations, resulting in a better document embedding. With the hierarchical variants, on the other hand, each sentence vector is produced in isolation, without any contextual information about the other sentences in the document. Therefore, the final sentence embeddings might be of lower quality, and as a group might also contain redundant/repeated information. When the sentence vectors are finally combined into a document representation, it is too late to take context into account.

Results and ablations ::: Ablation studies	To understand the impact of some hyperparameters on performance, we conducted additional experiments on the Reuters, Polarity, and IMDB datasets, with the non-hierarchical version of MPAD. Indeed, in initial experiments involving readout at $t$=$T$ only, setting $T\ge 2$ was always decreasing performance, despite the GRU-based updates (Eq. DISPLAY_FORM14). These results were consistent with that of  and , who both are reading out only at $t$=$T$ too. We hypothesize that node features at $T\ge 2$ are too diffuse to be entirely relied upon during readout. More precisely, initially at $t$=0, node representations capture information about words, at $t$=1, about their 1-hop neighborhood (bigrams), at $t$=2, about compositions of bigrams, etc. Thus, pretty quickly, node features become general and diffuse. In such cases, considering also the lower-level, more precise features of the earlier iterations when reading out may be necessary. Undirected edges. MPAD reaches best performance on 7 out of 10 datasets, and is close second elsewhere.

Results and ablations ::: Results	Experimental results are shown in Table TABREF28. For the baselines, the best scores reported in each original paper are shown. MPAD reaches best performance on 7 out of 10 datasets, and is close second elsewhere. Moreover, the 7 datasets on which MPAD ranks first widely differ in training set size, number of categories, and prediction task (topic, sentiment, subjectivity), which indicates that MPAD can perform well in different settings. MPAD vs. hierarchical variants. On 9 datasets out of 10, one or more of the hierarchical variants outperform the vanilla MPAD architecture, highlighting the benefit of explicitly modeling the hierarchical nature of documents. However, on Subjectivity, standard MPAD outperforms all hierarchical variants. On TREC, it reaches the same accuracy. We hypothesize that in some cases, using

a different graph to separately encode each sentence might be worse than using one single graph to directly encode the document. Indeed, in the single document graph, some words that never appear in the same sentence can be connected through common neighbors, as was explained in subsection SECREF7. So, this way, some notion of cross-sentence context is captured while learning representations of words, bigrams, etc. at each MP iteration. This creates better informed representations, resulting in a better document embedding. With the hierarchical variants, on the other hand, each sentence vector is produced in isolation, without any contextual information about the other sentences in the document. Therefore, the final sentence embeddings might be of lower quality, and as a group might also contain redundant/repeated information. When the sentence vectors are finally combined into a document representation, it is too late to take context into account.

Results and ablations ::: Ablation studies	To understand the impact of some hyperparameters on performance, we conducted additional experiments on the Reuters, Polarity, and IMDB datasets, with the non-hierarchical version of MPAD. All experiments were run on a single machine consisting of a 3.4 GHz Intel Core i7 CPU with 16 GB of RAM and an NVidia GeForce Titan Xp GPU.\n\nResults and ablations ::: Results\tExperimental results are shown in Table TABREF28. For the baselines, the best scores reported in each original paper are shown. MPAD reaches best performance on 7 out of 10 datasets, and is close second elsewhere. Moreover, the 7 datasets on which MPAD ranks first widely differ in training set size, number of categories, and prediction task (topic, sentiment, subjectivity), which indicates that MPAD can perform well in different settings. MPAD vs. hierarchical variants. On 9 datasets out of 10, one or more of the hierarchical variants outperform the vanilla MPAD architecture, highlighting the benefit of explicitly modeling the hierarchical nature of documents. However, on Subjectivity, standard MPAD outperforms all hierarchical variants. On TREC, it reaches the same accuracy. We hypothesize that in some cases, using&quot;

      &quot;tokens&quot;: 256,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;a different graph to separately encode each sentence might be worse than using one single graph to directly encode the document. Indeed, in the single document graph, some words that never appear in the same sentence can be connected through common neighbors, as was explained in subsection SECREF7. So, this way, some notion of cross-sentence context is captured while learning representations of words, bigrams, etc. at each MP iteration. This creates better informed representations, resulting in a better document embedding. With the hierarchical variants, on the other hand, each sentence vector is produced in isolation, without any contextual information about the other sentences in the document. Therefore, the final sentence embeddings might be of lower quality, and as a group might also contain redundant/repeated information. When the sentence vectors are finally combined into a document representation, it is too late to take context into account.\n\nResults and ablations ::: Ablation studies\tTo understand the impact of some hyperparameters on performance, we conducted additional experiments on the Reuters, Polarity, and IMDB datasets, with the non-hierarchical version of MPAD.       &quot;tokens&quot;: 256,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;state-of-the-art baseline models, including hierarchical ones, to enable fair comparison with the hierarchical MPAD variants. doc2vec . Doc2vec (or paragraph vector) is an extension of word2vec that learns vectors for documents in a fully unsupervised manner. Document embeddings are then fed to a logistic regression classifier. CNN . The convolutional neural network architecture, well-known in computer vision, is applied to text. There is one spatial dimension and the word embeddings are used as channels (depth dimensions). DAN . The Deep Averaging Network passes the unweighted average of the embeddings of the input words through multiple dense layers and a final softmax. Tree-LSTM  is a generalization of the standard LSTM architecture to constituency and dependency parse trees. DRNN . Recursive neural networks are stacked and applied to parse trees. LSTMN  is an extension of the LSTM model where the memory cell is replaced by a memory network which stores word representations. C-LSTM  combines convolutional and recurrent neural networks. The region embeddings provided by a CNN are fed to a LSTM. SPGK  also models documents as word co-occurrence networks. It computes a graph kernel that compares shortest paths extracted from the word co-occurrence networks and then uses a SVM to categorize&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;c27725b16464738b231ba1b7932415f7&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;c27725b16464738b231ba1b7932415f7&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1908.06267&quot;,

      &quot;start&quot;: 16181,
      &quot;end&quot;: 17322,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 254,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;documents. WMD  is an application of the well-known Earth Mover&#x27;s Distance to text. A k-nearest neighbor classifier is used. S-WMD  is a supervised extension of the Word Mover&#x27;s Distance. Semantic-CNN . Here, a CNN is applied to semantic units obtained by clustering words in the embedding space. LSTM-GRNN  is a hierarchical model where sentence embeddings are obtained with a CNN and a GRU-RNN is fed the sentence representations to obtain a document vector. HN-ATT  is another hierarchical model, where the same encoder architecture (a bidirectional GRU-RNN) is used for both sentences and documents, with different parameters. A self-attention mechanism is applied to the RNN annotations at each level.\n\nExperiments ::: Model configuration and training\tWe preprocess all datasets using the code of . On Yelp2013, we also replace all tokens appearing strictly less than 6 times with a special UNK token, like in . We then build a directed word co-occurrence network from each document, with a window of size 2. We use two MP iterations ($T$=2) for the basic MPAD, and two MP iterations at each level, for the hierarchical variants. We set&quot;

      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;learn our own word vectors from the training and validation sets with the gensim implementation of word2vec . MPAD was implemented in Python 3.6 using the PyTorch library . All experiments were run on a single machine consisting of a 3.4 GHz Intel Core i7 CPU with 16 GB of RAM and an NVidia GeForce Titan Xp GPU.\n\nResults and ablations ::: Results\tExperimental results are shown in Table TABREF28. For the baselines, the best scores reported in each original paper are shown. MPAD reaches best performance on 7 out of 10 datasets, and is close second elsewhere. Moreover, the 7 datasets on which MPAD ranks first widely differ in training set size, number of categories, and prediction task (topic, sentiment, subjectivity), which indicates that MPAD can perform well in different settings. MPAD vs. hierarchical variants. On 9 datasets out of 10, one or more of the hierarchical variants outperform the vanilla MPAD architecture, highlighting the benefit of explicitly modeling the hierarchical nature of documents. However, on Subjectivity, standard MPAD outperforms all hierarchical variants. On TREC, it reaches the same accuracy. We hypothesize that in some cases, using&quot;

A large majority of the errors come from misclassifying hateful categories (racism and sexism) as hatless (neither) and vice versa. 0.9% and 18.5% of all racism samples are misclassified as sexism and neither respectively whereas it is 0% and 12.7% for sexism samples. Almost 12% of neither samples are misclassified as racism or sexism. <pre>32 for 3 epochs. The dropout probability is set to 0.1 for all layers. Adam optimizer is used with a learning rate of 2e-5. As an input, we tokenized each tweet with the BERT tokenizer. As tweets are short texts, we set the maximum sequence length to 64 and in any shorter or longer length case it will be padded with zero values or truncated to the maximum length. We consider 80% of each dataset as training data to update the weights in the fine-tuning phase, 10% as validation data to measure the out-of-sample performance of the model during training, and 10% as test data to measure the out-of-sample performance after training. To prevent overfitting, we use stratified sampling to select 0.8, 0.1, and 0.1 portions of tweets from each class (racism/sexism/neither or hate/offensive/neither) for train, validation, and test. <pre>baselines. Using the pre-trained BERT model as initial embeddings and fine-tuning the model with a fully connected linear classifier (BERTbase) outperforms previous baselines yielding F1-score of 81% and 91% for datasets of Waseem and Davidson respectively. Inserting a CNN to pre-trained BERT model for fine-tuning on downstream task provides the best results as F1- score of 88% and 92% for datasets of Waseem and Davidson and it clearly exceeds the baselines. Intuitively, this makes sense that combining all pre-trained BERT layers with a CNN yields better results in which our model uses all the information included in different layers of pre-trained BERT during the fine-tuning phase. This information contains both syntactical and contextual features coming from lower layers to higher layers of BERT.

Experiments and Results ::: Pre-Processing	We find mentions of users, numbers, hashtags, URLs and common emoticons and replace them with the tokens &lt;user&gt;,&lt;number&gt;,&lt;hashtag&gt;,&lt;url&gt;,&lt;emoticon&gt;. We also find elongated words and convert them into short and standard format; for example, converting yeeeessss to yes. With hashtags that include some tokens without any with space between them, we replace them by their textual counterparts; for example, we convert hashtag “#notsexist&quot; to “not sexist&quot;. All punctuation marks, unknown uni-codes and extra delimiting characters are removed, but we keep all stop words because our model trains the sequence of words in a text directly. We also convert all tweets to lower case.

Experiments and Results ::: Dataset Description	We evaluate our method on two

widely-studied datasets provided by Waseem and Hovey  and Davidson et al. .

To extend this dataset, Waseem  also provided another dataset containing $6.9k$ of tweets annotated with both expert and crowdsourcing users as racism, sexism, neither, or both.

As the implementation environment, we use Google Colaboratory tool which is a free research tool with a Tesla K80 GPU and 12G RAM.

As it is understandable from Tables TABREF16(classdistributionwaseem) and TABREF16(classdistributiondavidson), we are dealing with imbalance datasets with various classes’ distribution.

The evaluation results are reported on the test dataset and on three different metrics: precision, recall, and weighted-average F1-score.</pre></details></td></tr></tbody></table>

Experiments and Results	We first introduce datasets used in our study and then investigate the different fine-tuning strategies for hate speech detection task.

Experiments and Results ::: Dataset Description	We evaluate our method on two

widely-studied datasets provided by Waseem and Hovey  and Davidson et al. .

Waseem and Hovy  collected $16k$ of tweets based on an initial ad-hoc approach that searched common slurs and terms related to religious, sexual, gender, and ethnic minorities.

They annotated their dataset manually as racism, sexism, or neither.

To extend this dataset, Waseem  also provided another dataset containing $6.9k$ of tweets annotated with both expert and crowdsourcing users as racism, sexism, neither, or both.

Since both datasets are overlapped partially and they used the same strategy in definition of hateful content, we merged these two datasets following Waseem et al.  to make our imbalance data a bit larger.

Davidson et al.  used the Twitter API to accumulate 84.4 million tweets from 33,458 twitter users containing particular terms from a pre-defined lexicon of hate speech words and phrases, called Hatebased.org.

To annotate collected tweets as Hate, Offensive, or Neither, they randomly sampled $25k$ tweets and asked users of CrowdFlower crowdsourcing platform to label them.

In detail, the distribution of different classes in both datasets will be provided

As the implementation environment, we use Google Colaboratory tool which is a free research tool with a Tesla K80 GPU and 12G RAM.

We consider 80% of each dataset as training data to update the weights in the fine-tuning phase, 10% as validation data to measure the out-of-sample performance of the model during training, and 10% as test data to measure the out-of-sample performance after training.

To prevent overfitting, we use stratified sampling to select 0.8, 0.1, and 0.1 portions of tweets from each class (racism/sexism/neither or hate/offensive/neither) for train, validation, and test.

Classes&#x27; distribution of train, validation, and test datasets are shown

As it is understandable from Tables TABREF16(classdistributionwaseem) and TABREF16(classdistributiondavidson), we are dealing with imbalance datasets with various classes’ distribution.

Since hate speech and offensive languages are real phenomena, we did not perform oversampling or undersampling techniques to adjust the classes’ distribution and tried to supply the datasets as realistic as possible.

We use Waseem and Hovy , Davidson et al. , and Waseem et al.  as baselines and compare the results with our different fine-tuning strategies using pre-trained BERTbase model.

The evaluation results are reported on the test dataset and on three different metrics: precision, recall, and weighted-average F1-score.

Inserting a CNN to pre-trained BERT model for fine-tuning on downstream task provides the best results as F1- score of 88% and 92% for datasets of Waseem and Davidson and it clearly exceeds the baselines.

We investigate the test datasets and their confusion matrices resulted from the BERTbase + CNN model as the best fine-tuning approach;

Insert CNN layer: In this architecture shown in Figure FIGREF8, the outputs of all transformer encoders are used instead of using the output of the latest transformer encoder. So that the output vectors of each transformer encoder are concatenated, and a matrix is produced.       &quot;text&quot;: &quot;classifiers trained on datasets containing more implicit abuse (tweets with some abusive words) are more affected by biases rather than once trained on datasets with a high proportion of explicit abuse samples (tweets containing sarcasm, jokes, etc.).&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;682b3d416054bd587a763f2f16f4bb38&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;55b5496ee1930a9d7a72ecb7bd6cc5a5&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1910.12574&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 15719,
      &quot;end&quot;: 15841,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 29,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;such a way that they are given as inputs to a bidirectional recurrent neural network (Bi-LSTM) as shown in Figure FIGREF8.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;88e6eb4cb47e4881582e341217b41809&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;55b5496ee1930a9d7a72ecb7bd6cc5a5&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1910.12574&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 16008,
      &quot;end&quot;: 16010,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 2,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;4.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;1bf027303edbb47bd8b3ec5ac4221cc7&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;55b5496ee1930a9d7a72ecb7bd6cc5a5&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1910.12574&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 16705,
      &quot;end&quot;: 16864,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 28,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Experiments and Results\tWe first introduce datasets used in our study and then investigate the different fine-tuning strategies for hate speech detection task.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;875fa8d812d1ff95e4ff88100b991caf&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;55b5496ee1930a9d7a72ecb7bd6cc5a5&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1910.12574&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 16966,
      &quot;end&quot;: 17043,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 14,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Experiments and Results ::: Dataset Description\tWe evaluate our method on two&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;e284b75fd75ccc542fefb2fdafd803f3&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;5e6211bd5861a3d7a14c013e35cdbe8f&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1910.12574&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 17044,
      &quot;end&quot;: 17119,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 22,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;widely-studied datasets provided by Waseem and Hovey  and Davidson et al. .&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;12d10418c8ec84bedc8bb02a03ca789c&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;5e6211bd5861a3d7a14c013e35cdbe8f&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1910.12574&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 17120,
      &quot;end&quot;: 17296,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 42,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Waseem and Hovy  collected $16k$ of tweets based on an initial ad-hoc approach that searched common slurs and terms related to religious, sexual, gender, and ethnic minorities.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;1b478c8d4b281785d818a7066d5255fa&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;5e6211bd5861a3d7a14c013e35cdbe8f&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1910.12574&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 17297,
      &quot;end&quot;: 17365,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 13,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;They annotated their dataset manually as racism, sexism, or neither.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;21563b103f224f70adb9761b61bfbe32&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;5e6211bd5861a3d7a14c013e35cdbe8f&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1910.12574&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 17366,
      &quot;end&quot;: 17543,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 40,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;To extend this dataset, Waseem  also provided another dataset containing $6.9k$ of tweets annotated with both expert and crowdsourcing users as racism, sexism, neither, or both.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;909bace23409361abbdb3e732c2320b2&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;5e6211bd5861a3d7a14c013e35cdbe8f&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1910.12574&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 17544,
      &quot;end&quot;: 17749,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 41,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Since both datasets are overlapped partially and they used the same strategy in definition of hateful content, we merged these two datasets following Waseem et al.  to make our imbalance data a bit larger.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;18eeca36612e91fa0aef67919f854cbe&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;5e6211bd5861a3d7a14c013e35cdbe8f&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1910.12574&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 17750,
      &quot;end&quot;: 17958,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 50,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Davidson et al.  used the Twitter API to accumulate 84.4 million tweets from 33,458 twitter users containing particular terms from a pre-defined lexicon of hate speech words and phrases, called Hatebased.org.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;f9e5182b408acad7e91362124da53a1e&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;5e6211bd5861a3d7a14c013e35cdbe8f&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1910.12574&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 17959,
      &quot;end&quot;: 18123,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 35,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;To annotate collected tweets as Hate, Offensive, or Neither, they randomly sampled $25k$ tweets and asked users of CrowdFlower crowdsourcing platform to label them.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;15f94b41dba4ba9c34e890a46a3d1faa&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;5e6211bd5861a3d7a14c013e35cdbe8f&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1910.12574&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 18124,
      &quot;end&quot;: 18206,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 14,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;In detail, the distribution of different classes in both datasets will be provided&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;297a11d6b3ecba50605f0bd4183dc846&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;44d25073f18a993402d63955d8b0ea92&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1910.12574&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 19184,
      &quot;end&quot;: 19314,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 32,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;As the implementation environment, we use Google Colaboratory tool which is a free research tool with a Tesla K80 GPU and 12G RAM.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;796b81decfd87bce8ee7cf46e96bab58&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;81631426cb5c6a74021aa8070d0d78f0&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1910.12574&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 19935,
      &quot;end&quot;: 20203,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 61,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;We consider 80% of each dataset as training data to update the weights in the fine-tuning phase, 10% as validation data to measure the out-of-sample performance of the model during training, and 10% as test data to measure the out-of-sample performance after training.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;7362a7d521649f5070d1bfc0a928123e&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;81631426cb5c6a74021aa8070d0d78f0&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1910.12574&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 20204,
      &quot;end&quot;: 20400,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 57,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;To prevent overfitting, we use stratified sampling to select 0.8, 0.1, and 0.1 portions of tweets from each class (racism/sexism/neither or hate/offensive/neither) for train, validation, and test.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;2aaceed1c3bffc67b3131f6de5a53b70&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;81631426cb5c6a74021aa8070d0d78f0&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1910.12574&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 20401,
      &quot;end&quot;: 20472,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 13,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Classes&#x27; distribution of train, validation, and test datasets are shown&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;78efdb9e6c5360a04d8b8b90126960ad&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;2bda4718c14fff07b9d5e329a56693e1&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1910.12574&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 20492,
      &quot;end&quot;: 20677,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 39,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;As it is understandable from Tables TABREF16(classdistributionwaseem) and TABREF16(classdistributiondavidson), we are dealing with imbalance datasets with various classes’ distribution.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;94605d61f87a012abbb8c95abf5a10dc&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;2bda4718c14fff07b9d5e329a56693e1&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1910.12574&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 20678,
      &quot;end&quot;: 20894,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 37,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Since hate speech and offensive languages are real phenomena, we did not perform oversampling or undersampling techniques to adjust the classes’ distribution and tried to supply the datasets as realistic as possible.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;02308b5aa05d98def17535e7d799da56&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;2bda4718c14fff07b9d5e329a56693e1&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1910.12574&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 21096,
      &quot;end&quot;: 21270,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 44,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;We use Waseem and Hovy , Davidson et al. , and Waseem et al.  as baselines and compare the results with our different fine-tuning strategies using pre-trained BERTbase model.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;bc0c838efcb1ae8ecfc5861eeeb2c366&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;2bda4718c14fff07b9d5e329a56693e1&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1910.12574&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 21271,
      &quot;end&quot;: 21408,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 26,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;The evaluation results are reported on the test dataset and on three different metrics: precision, recall, and weighted-average F1-score.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;dc34abe7ac3dc19d8032df492b373bf5&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;bf18889e9741fda4ae53bc2bb8203f3c&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1910.12574&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 21712,
      &quot;end&quot;: 21722,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 3,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;baselines.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;e79ed48071072bc4663cc5a60916a545&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;bf18889e9741fda4ae53bc2bb8203f3c&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1910.12574&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 21723,
      &quot;end&quot;: 21969,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 56,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Using the pre-trained BERT model as initial embeddings and fine-tuning the model with a fully connected linear classifier (BERTbase) outperforms previous baselines yielding F1-score of 81% and 91% for datasets of Waseem and Davidson respectively.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;453471aa21221f171189be12dc670e99&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;bf18889e9741fda4ae53bc2bb8203f3c&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1910.12574&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 21970,
      &quot;end&quot;: 22174,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 52,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Inserting a CNN to pre-trained BERT model for fine-tuning on downstream task provides the best results as F1- score of 88% and 92% for datasets of Waseem and Davidson and it clearly exceeds the baselines.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;88f732c400291d1b825a92b08bcb4375&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;bf18889e9741fda4ae53bc2bb8203f3c&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1910.12574&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 22808,
      &quot;end&quot;: 22942,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 26,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;We investigate the test datasets and their confusion matrices resulted from the BERTbase + CNN model as the best fine-tuning approach;&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;07671839531c9726cfae3e44a2b54533&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;59e412de484d341b40a989f46ac78baf&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1910.12574&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 22986,
      &quot;end&quot;: 23113,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 28,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;According to Figure FIGREF19 for Waseem-dataset, it is obvious that the model can separate sexism from racism content properly.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;e180c433a014d012cd336e9276f6592d&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;59e412de484d341b40a989f46ac78baf&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1910.12574&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 23850,
      &quot;end&quot;: 24013,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 40,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;To understand better the mislabeled items by our model, we did a manual inspection on a subset of the data and record some of them in Tables TABREF20 and TABREF21.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;6188ab9d2f7b50da99fc505523687cb2&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;633e8e3d71c30e203d437a8c6c30fd4e&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1910.12574&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 24627,
      &quot;end&quot;: 24820,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 38,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;By examining more samples and with respect to recently studies , , , it is clear that many errors are due to biases from data collection  and rules of annotation  and not the classifier itself.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;e6bea637579f8e745f0feca13f832b9e&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;633e8e3d71c30e203d437a8c6c30fd4e&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1910.12574&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 24821,
      &quot;end&quot;: 25047,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 51,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Since Waseem et al. created a small ad-hoc set of keywords and Davidson et al. used a large crowdsourced dictionary of keywords (Hatebase lexicon) to sample tweets for training, they included some biases in the collected data.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;aee84b512e826f3440d2216cf5630b0d&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;633e8e3d71c30e203d437a8c6c30fd4e&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1910.12574&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 25048,
      &quot;end&quot;: 25278,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 40,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Especially for Davidson-dataset, some tweets with specific language (written within the African American Vernacular English) and geographic restriction (United States of America) are oversampled such as tweets containing disparage&quot;
    }
  ],

      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;5e6211bd5861a3d7a14c013e35cdbe8f&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;5e6211bd5861a3d7a14c013e35cdbe8f&quot;,

      &quot;tokens&quot;: 256,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;widely-studied datasets provided by Waseem and Hovey  and Davidson et al. . Waseem and Hovy  collected $16k$ of tweets based on an initial ad-hoc approach that searched common slurs and terms related to religious, sexual, gender, and ethnic minorities. They annotated their dataset manually as racism, sexism, or neither. To extend this dataset, Waseem  also provided another dataset containing $6.9k$ of tweets annotated with both expert and crowdsourcing users as racism, sexism, neither, or both. Since both datasets are overlapped partially and they used the same strategy in definition of hateful content, we merged these two datasets following Waseem et al.  to make our imbalance data a bit larger. Davidson et al.  used the Twitter API to accumulate 84.4 million tweets from 33,458 twitter users containing particular terms from a pre-defined lexicon of hate speech words and phrases, called Hatebased.org. To annotate collected tweets as Hate, Offensive, or Neither, they randomly sampled $25k$ tweets and asked users of CrowdFlower crowdsourcing platform to label them. In detail, the distribution of different classes in both datasets will be provided&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;297a11d6b3ecba50605f0bd4183dc846&quot;,

      &quot;tokens&quot;: 256,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;32 for 3 epochs. The dropout probability is set to 0.1 for all layers. Adam optimizer is used with a learning rate of 2e-5. As an input, we tokenized each tweet with the BERT tokenizer. It contains invalid characters removal, punctuation splitting, and lowercasing the words. Based on the original BERT , we split words to subword units using WordPiece tokenization. As tweets are short texts, we set the maximum sequence length to 64 and in any shorter or longer length case it will be padded with zero values or truncated to the maximum length. We consider 80% of each dataset as training data to update the weights in the fine-tuning phase, 10% as validation data to measure the out-of-sample performance of the model during training, and 10% as test data to measure the out-of-sample performance after training. To prevent overfitting, we use stratified sampling to select 0.8, 0.1, and 0.1 portions of tweets from each class (racism/sexism/neither or hate/offensive/neither) for train, validation, and test. Classes&#x27; distribution of train, validation, and test datasets are shown&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;59e412de484d341b40a989f46ac78baf&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;59e412de484d341b40a989f46ac78baf&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1910.12574&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;PASSAGE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 22943,
      &quot;end&quot;: 24013,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 256,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;depicted in Figures FIGREF19 and FIGREF19. According to Figure FIGREF19 for Waseem-dataset, it is obvious that the model can separate sexism from racism content properly. Only two samples belonging to racism class are misclassified as sexism and none of the sexism samples are misclassified as racism. A large majority of the errors come from misclassifying hateful categories (racism and sexism) as hatless (neither) and vice versa. 0.9% and 18.5% of all racism samples are misclassified as sexism and neither respectively whereas it is 0% and 12.7% for sexism samples. Almost 12% of neither samples are misclassified as racism or sexism. As Figure FIGREF19 makes clear for Davidson-dataset, the majority of errors are related to hate class where the model misclassified hate content as offensive in 63% of the cases. However, 2.6% and 7.9% of offensive and neither samples are misclassified respectively. To understand better the mislabeled items by our model, we did a manual inspection on a subset of the data and record some of them in Tables TABREF20 and TABREF21.&quot;

      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;such a way that they are given as inputs to a bidirectional recurrent neural network (Bi-LSTM) as shown in Figure FIGREF8. After processing the input, the network sends the final hidden state to a fully connected network that performs classification using the softmax activation function. 4. Insert CNN layer: In this architecture shown in Figure FIGREF8, the outputs of all transformer encoders are used instead of using the output of the latest transformer encoder. So that the output vectors of each transformer encoder are concatenated, and a matrix is produced. The convolutional operation is performed with a window of size (3, hidden size of BERT which is 768 in BERTbase model) and the maximum value is generated for each transformer encoder by applying max pooling on the convolution output. By concatenating these values, a vector is generated which is given as input to a fully connected network. By applying softmax on the input, the classification operation is performed.\n\nExperiments and Results\tWe first introduce datasets used in our study and then investigate the different fine-tuning strategies for hate speech detection task. We also include the details of our implementation and error analysis in the respective subsections.\n\nExperiments and Results ::: Dataset Description\tWe evaluate our method on two&quot;

      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;To extend this dataset, Waseem  also provided another dataset containing $6.9k$ of tweets annotated with both expert and crowdsourcing users as racism, sexism, neither, or both.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;909bace23409361abbdb3e732c2320b2&quot;,

    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;18eeca36612e91fa0aef67919f854cbe&quot;,

      &quot;tokens&quot;: 50,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Davidson et al.  used the Twitter API to accumulate 84.4 million tweets from 33,458 twitter users containing particular terms from a pre-defined lexicon of hate speech words and phrases, called Hatebased.org.&quot;

    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;297a11d6b3ecba50605f0bd4183dc846&quot;,

      &quot;end&quot;: 19314,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 32,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;As the implementation environment, we use Google Colaboratory tool which is a free research tool with a Tesla K80 GPU and 12G RAM.&quot;
    },

      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;81631426cb5c6a74021aa8070d0d78f0&quot;,

      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;32 for 3 epochs. The dropout probability is set to 0.1 for all layers. Adam optimizer is used with a learning rate of 2e-5. As an input, we tokenized each tweet with the BERT tokenizer. It contains invalid characters removal, punctuation splitting, and lowercasing the words. Based on the original BERT , we split words to subword units using WordPiece tokenization. As tweets are short texts, we set the maximum sequence length to 64 and in any shorter or longer length case it will be padded with zero values or truncated to the maximum length. We consider 80% of each dataset as training data to update the weights in the fine-tuning phase, 10% as validation data to measure the out-of-sample performance of the model during training, and 10% as test data to measure the out-of-sample performance after training. To prevent overfitting, we use stratified sampling to select 0.8, 0.1, and 0.1 portions of tweets from each class (racism/sexism/neither or hate/offensive/neither) for train, validation, and test. Classes&#x27; distribution of train, validation, and test datasets are shown&quot;

#### What V1 discarded / V2 recovered

<pre>{
  &quot;FIXED_SENTENCE_sentences_absent_in_V1&quot;: [
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;02308b5aa05d98def17535e7d799da56&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;2bda4718c14fff07b9d5e329a56693e1&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;We use Waseem and Hovy , Davidson et al. , and Waseem et al.  as baselines and compare the results with our different fine-tuning strategies using pre-trained BERTbase model.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;07671839531c9726cfae3e44a2b54533&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;59e412de484d341b40a989f46ac78baf&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;According to Figure FIGREF19 for Waseem-dataset, it is obvious that the model can separate sexism from racism content properly.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;12d10418c8ec84bedc8bb02a03ca789c&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;5e6211bd5861a3d7a14c013e35cdbe8f&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Waseem and Hovy  collected $16k$ of tweets based on an initial ad-hoc approach that searched common slurs and terms related to religious, sexual, gender, and ethnic minorities.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;14473ecead7ae5b7039fbafca7c5c5c8&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;996bdf59568096558d72b3c649b588fa&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;classifiers trained on datasets containing more implicit abuse (tweets with some abusive words) are more affected by biases rather than once trained on datasets with a high proportion of explicit abuse samples (tweets containing sarcasm, jokes, etc.).&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;18eeca36612e91fa0aef67919f854cbe&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;5e6211bd5861a3d7a14c013e35cdbe8f&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Davidson et al.  used the Twitter API to accumulate 84.4 million tweets from 33,458 twitter users containing particular terms from a pre-defined lexicon of hate speech words and phrases, called Hatebased.org.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;1bf027303edbb47bd8b3ec5ac4221cc7&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;55b5496ee1930a9d7a72ecb7bd6cc5a5&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Experiments and Results\tWe first introduce datasets used in our study and then investigate the different fine-tuning strategies for hate speech detection task.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;21563b103f224f70adb9761b61bfbe32&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;5e6211bd5861a3d7a14c013e35cdbe8f&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;To extend this dataset, Waseem  also provided another dataset containing $6.9k$ of tweets annotated with both expert and crowdsourcing users as racism, sexism, neither, or both.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;297a11d6b3ecba50605f0bd4183dc846&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;44d25073f18a993402d63955d8b0ea92&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;As the implementation environment, we use Google Colaboratory tool which is a free research tool with a Tesla K80 GPU and 12G RAM.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;453471aa21221f171189be12dc670e99&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;bf18889e9741fda4ae53bc2bb8203f3c&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Inserting a CNN to pre-trained BERT model for fine-tuning on downstream task provides the best results as F1- score of 88% and 92% for datasets of Waseem and Davidson and it clearly exceeds the baselines.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;6188ab9d2f7b50da99fc505523687cb2&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;633e8e3d71c30e203d437a8c6c30fd4e&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;By examining more samples and with respect to recently studies , , , it is clear that many errors are due to biases from data collection  and rules of annotation  and not the classifier itself.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;682b3d416054bd587a763f2f16f4bb38&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;55b5496ee1930a9d7a72ecb7bd6cc5a5&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;such a way that they are given as inputs to a bidirectional recurrent neural network (Bi-LSTM) as shown in Figure FIGREF8.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;7362a7d521649f5070d1bfc0a928123e&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;81631426cb5c6a74021aa8070d0d78f0&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;To prevent overfitting, we use stratified sampling to select 0.8, 0.1, and 0.1 portions of tweets from each class (racism/sexism/neither or hate/offensive/neither) for train, validation, and test.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;78efdb9e6c5360a04d8b8b90126960ad&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;2bda4718c14fff07b9d5e329a56693e1&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;As it is understandable from Tables TABREF16(classdistributionwaseem) and TABREF16(classdistributiondavidson), we are dealing with imbalance datasets with various classes’ distribution.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;796b81decfd87bce8ee7cf46e96bab58&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;81631426cb5c6a74021aa8070d0d78f0&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;We consider 80% of each dataset as training data to update the weights in the fine-tuning phase, 10% as validation data to measure the out-of-sample performance of the model during training, and 10% as test data to measure the out-of-sample performance after training.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;88f732c400291d1b825a92b08bcb4375&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;bf18889e9741fda4ae53bc2bb8203f3c&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;We investigate the test datasets and their confusion matrices resulted from the BERTbase + CNN model as the best fine-tuning approach;&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;909bace23409361abbdb3e732c2320b2&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;5e6211bd5861a3d7a14c013e35cdbe8f&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Since both datasets are overlapped partially and they used the same strategy in definition of hateful content, we merged these two datasets following Waseem et al.  to make our imbalance data a bit larger.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;94605d61f87a012abbb8c95abf5a10dc&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;2bda4718c14fff07b9d5e329a56693e1&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Since hate speech and offensive languages are real phenomena, we did not perform oversampling or undersampling techniques to adjust the classes’ distribution and tried to supply the datasets as realistic as possible.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;aee84b512e826f3440d2216cf5630b0d&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;633e8e3d71c30e203d437a8c6c30fd4e&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Especially for Davidson-dataset, some tweets with specific language (written within the African American Vernacular English) and geographic restriction (United States of America) are oversampled such as tweets containing disparage&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;bc0c838efcb1ae8ecfc5861eeeb2c366&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;2bda4718c14fff07b9d5e329a56693e1&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;The evaluation results are reported on the test dataset and on three different metrics: precision, recall, and weighted-average F1-score.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;e180c433a014d012cd336e9276f6592d&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;59e412de484d341b40a989f46ac78baf&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;To understand better the mislabeled items by our model, we did a manual inspection on a subset of the data and record some of them in Tables TABREF20 and TABREF21.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;e6bea637579f8e745f0feca13f832b9e&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;633e8e3d71c30e203d437a8c6c30fd4e&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Since Waseem et al. created a small ad-hoc set of keywords and Davidson et al. used a large crowdsourced dictionary of keywords (Hatebase lexicon) to sample tweets for training, they included some biases in the collected data.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;e79ed48071072bc4663cc5a60916a545&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;bf18889e9741fda4ae53bc2bb8203f3c&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Using the pre-trained BERT model as initial embeddings and fine-tuning the model with a fully connected linear classifier (BERTbase) outperforms previous baselines yielding F1-score of 81% and 91% for datasets of Waseem and Davidson respectively.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;f9e5182b408acad7e91362124da53a1e&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;5e6211bd5861a3d7a14c013e35cdbe8f&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;To annotate collected tweets as Hate, Offensive, or Neither, they randomly sampled $25k$ tweets and asked users of CrowdFlower crowdsourcing platform to label them.&quot;
    }
  ],
  &quot;QBGF_FULL_sentences_absent_in_V1&quot;: [

    {

      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Experiments and Results\tWe first introduce datasets used in our study and then investigate the different fine-tuning strategies for hate speech detection task.&quot;
    },
    {
