<pre>{
  &quot;FIXED_SENTENCE_sentences_absent_in_V1&quot;: [
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;04d64e5b772ecfbb3bb908e911175de9&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;ce9eb0bf7459dbde38cd00c648084c58&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;We assessed in a comprehensive and nonbiased manner the IgA anti-TG2 response by expression cloning of the antibody repertoire of ex vivo–isolated intestinal antibody-secreting cells (ASCs).&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;08cea08c11b35036cf3030e859bb8006&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;383bac23b6cd85aee72c08ba81a437ae&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;The effects of purified celiac IgA and monoclonal tissue transglutaminase antibodies (CUB7402) were studied by adding the antibodies to the cocultures.   \n&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;2367f1949074d7f840228a692cca4ded&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;97c6f43fffe9dfb6e1ca038c8de73164&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;One was the antitissue transglutaminase antibodies (AtTGA) stick for IgA/G antibodies to tTG detection, the other was the AtTGA/antigliadin antibodies (AGA) stick for IgA antibodies for tTG and/or gliadins.   \n&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;3f1f752a224ea3789d9e5bd7a4d25823&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;75686dc0a45e44eac48cdce5ce62edea&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Oat intolerance may be a reason for villous atrophy and inflammation in patients with celiac disease who are eating oats but otherwise are adhering to a strict gluten-free diet.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;52378713390d625c099f34f85d1a327b&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;383bac23b6cd85aee72c08ba81a437ae&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;CONCLUSIONS Celiac disease-associated IgA class antibodies disturb transforming growth factor beta-mediated fibroblast-epithelial cell cross-talk in this in vitro crypt-villus axis model.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;575f7b21693784a1d54905d9a2a4980e&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;ce9eb0bf7459dbde38cd00c648084c58&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Celiac disease is an immune-mediated disorder in which mucosal autoantibodies to the enzyme transglutaminase 2 (TG2) are generated in response to the exogenous antigen gluten in individuals who express human leukocyte antigen HLA-DQ2 or HLA-DQ8 (ref.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;592384653d20fa75f1c6206995f281f2&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;c2b44b3177833a3775f03e0f18edb675&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Predominance of Type 1 Innate Lymphoid Cells in the Rectal Mucosa of Patients With Non-Celiac Wheat Sensitivity: Reversal After a Wheat-Free Diet&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;5c3339ea66fa6697486a6916fcaa918a&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;75686dc0a45e44eac48cdce5ce62edea&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Deamidation (glutamine→glutamic acid conversion) by tissue transglutaminase was involved in the avenin epitope formation.      &quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;646ba6b87a76179541d5c955688cf7d9&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;ce9eb0bf7459dbde38cd00c648084c58&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;This could result in preferential recruitment of plasma cells from naive IgD- and IgM-expressing B cells, thus possibly explaining why the antibody response to TG2 bears signs of a primary immune response despite the disease chronicity.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;72bcaa1dd8cc19231d398c29a5e47c83&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;383bac23b6cd85aee72c08ba81a437ae&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;RESULTS Active celiac disease IgA, reactive for tissue transglutaminase, significantly inhibited T84 epithelial cell differentiation (P &lt; 0.001) and increased epithelial cell proliferation (P = 0.024).&quot;
    },

<details><summary>Rank 1 · 732c3dbcb31d77a82edcf27b27f8d608 · document 41982985 · score 0.80335 · 158 tokens</summary>

<pre>Altered TCR signaling from geometrically repatterned immunological synapses.
The immunological synapse is a specialized cell-cell junction that is defined by large-scale spatial patterns of receptors and signaling molecules yet remains largely enigmatic in terms of formation and function.
We used supported bilayer membranes and nanometer-scale structures fabricated onto the underlying substrate to impose geometric constraints on immunological synapse formation.
Analysis of the resulting alternatively patterned synapses revealed a causal relation between the radial position of T cell receptors (TCRs) and signaling activity, with prolonged signaling from TCR microclusters that had been mechanically trapped in the peripheral regions of the synapse.
These results are consistent with a model of the synapse in which spatial translocation of TCRs represents a direct mechanism of signal regulation.</pre>

</details>

<details><summary>Rank 2 · a67ce222cd70843cf45cb79234889e9c · document 15972906 · score 0.78475 · 215 tokens</summary>

<pre>Functional anatomy of T cell activation and synapse formation.
T cell activation and function require a structured engagement of antigen-presenting cells.
These cell contacts are characterized by two distinct dynamics in vivo: transient contacts resulting from promigratory junctions called immunological kinapses or prolonged contacts from stable junctions called immunological synapses.
Kinapses operate in the steady state to allow referencing to self-peptide-MHC (pMHC) and searching for pathogen-derived pMHC.
Synapses are induced by T cell receptor (TCR) interactions with agonist pMHC under specific conditions and correlate with robust immune responses that generate effector and memory T cells.
High-resolution imaging has revealed that the synapse is highly coordinated, integrating cell adhesion, TCR recognition of pMHC complexes, and an array of activating and inhibitory ligands to promote or prevent T cell signaling.
In this review, we examine the molecular components, geometry, and timing underlying kinapses and synapses.
We integrate recent molecular and physiological data to provide a synthesis and suggest ways forward.</pre>

</details>

<details><summary>Rank 3 · 2303c32e96b778bf583b74fbd1b9d5f9 · document 21746539 · score 0.78218 · 131 tokens</summary>

<pre>T-cell-antigen recognition and the immunological synapse
Much excitement of the past five years in the area of T-cell-antigen recognition has centred around the immunological synapse — a complex cellular structure that forms at the interface of a T cell and a cell that expresses the appropriate peptide–MHC complexes.
Thanks to new imaging technologies, we are now beginning to understand the role of cell-surface molecules and some of their attendant signalling modules in the context of cell-to-cell communication.
Progress has been so rapid that T-cell-antigen recognition might be the first system in which the molecular basis of cell–cell recognition is understood.</pre>

</details>

<details><summary>Rank 4 · 8222881e245779d31fa4c7615e05cb3c · document 4422734 · score 0.77610 · 205 tokens</summary>

<pre>Direct observation of ligand recognition by T cells
The activation of T cells through interaction of their T-cell receptors with antigenic peptide bound to major histocompatibility complex (MHC) on the surface of antigen presenting cells (APCs) is a crucial step in adaptive immunity.
Here we use three-dimensional fluorescence microscopy to visualize individual peptide–I-Ek class II MHC complexes labelled with the phycobiliprotein phycoerythrin in an effort to characterize T-cell sensitivity and the requirements for forming an immunological synapse in single cells.
We show that T cells expressing the CD4 antigen respond with transient calcium signalling to even a single agonist peptide–MHC ligand, and that the organization of molecules in the contact zone of the T cell and APC takes on the characteristics of an immunological synapse when only about ten agonists are present.
This sensitivity is highly dependant on CD4, because blocking this molecule with antibodies renders T cells unable to detect less than about 30 ligands.</pre>

</details>

<details><summary>Rank 5 · 42d84dabd5a8343f1479509b53552582 · document 18758057 · score 0.77581 · 483 tokens</summary>

<pre>NSOM/QD-Based Direct Visualization of CD3-Induced and CD28-Enhanced Nanospatial Coclustering of TCR and Coreceptor in Nanodomains in T Cell Activation
Direct molecular imaging of nano-spatial relationship between T cell receptor (TCR)/CD3 and CD4 or CD8 co-receptor before and after activation of a primary T cell has not been reported.
We have recently innovated application of near-field scanning optical microscopy (NSOM) and immune-labeling quantum dots (QD) to image Ag-specific TCR response during in vivo clonal expansion, and now up-graded the NSOM/QD-based nanotechnology through dipole-polarization and dual-color imaging.
Using this imaging system scanning cell-membrane molecules at a best-optical lateral resolution, we demonstrated that CD3, CD4 or CD8 molecules were distinctly distributed as single QD-bound molecules or nano-clusters equivalent to 2-4 QD fluorescence-intensity/size on cell-membrane of un-stimulated primary T cells, and approximately 6-10% of CD3 were co-clustering with CD4 or CD8 as 70-110 nm nano-clusters without forming nano-domains.
The ligation of TCR/CD3 on CD4 or CD8 T cells led to CD3 nanoscale co-clustering or interaction with CD4 or CD8 co-receptors forming 200-500 nm nano-domains or &gt;500 nm micro-domains.
Such nano-spatial co-clustering of CD3 and CD4 or CD3 and CD8 appeared to be an intrinsic event of TCR/CD3 ligation, not purely limited to MHC engagement, and be driven by Lck phosphorylation.
Importantly, CD28 co-stimulation remarkably enhanced TCR/CD3 nanoscale co-clustering or interaction with CD4 co-receptor within nano- or micro-domains on the membrane.
In contrast, CD28 co-stimulation did not enhance CD8 clustering or CD3-CD8 co-clustering in nano-domains although it increased molecular number and density of CD3 clustering in the enlarged nano-domains.
These nanoscale findings provide new insights into TCR/CD3 interaction with CD4 or CD8 co-receptor in T-cell activation.</pre>

</details>

<details><summary>Rank 6 · b9479b9dcbdfb5236a5ff7cbe8d0f84b · document 2714623 · score 0.77147 · 213 tokens</summary>

<pre>Recruitment of Nck by CD3ϵ Reveals a Ligand-Induced Conformational Change Essential for T Cell Receptor Signaling and Synapse Formation
How membrane receptors initiate signal transduction upon ligand binding is a matter of intense scrutiny.
The T cell receptor complex (TCR-CD3) is composed of TCR alpha/beta ligand binding subunits bound to the CD3 subunits responsible for signal transduction.
Although it has long been speculated that TCR-CD3 may undergo a conformational change, confirmation is still lacking.
We present strong evidence that ligand engagement of TCR-CD3 induces a conformational change that exposes a proline-rich sequence in CD3 epsilon and results in recruitment of the adaptor protein Nck.
This occurs earlier than and independently of tyrosine kinase activation.
Finally, by interfering with Nck-CD3 epsilon association in vivo, we demonstrate that TCR-CD3 recruitment of Nck is critical for maturation of the immune synapse and for T cell activation.</pre>

</details>

<details><summary>Rank 7 · 491f59498cad06f42087657a5fa9726f · document 5914739 · score 0.76813 · 286 tokens</summary>

<pre>Local changes in lipid environment of TCR microclusters regulate membrane binding by the CD3ε cytoplasmic domain
The CD3ε and ζ cytoplasmic domains of the T cell receptor bind to the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane (PM), and a previous nuclear magnetic resonance structure showed that both tyrosines of the CD3ε immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activation motif partition into the bilayer.
Electrostatic interactions between acidic phospholipids and clusters of basic CD3ε residues were previously shown to be essential for CD3ε and ζ membrane binding.
Phosphatidylserine (PS) is the most abundant negatively charged lipid on the inner leaflet of the PM and makes a major contribution to membrane binding by the CD3ε cytoplasmic domain.
Here, we show that TCR triggering by peptide--MHC complexes induces dissociation of the CD3ε cytoplasmic domain from the plasma membrane.
Release of the CD3ε cytoplasmic domain from the membrane is accompanied by a substantial focal reduction in negative charge and available PS in TCR microclusters.
These changes in the lipid composition of TCR microclusters even occur when TCR signaling is blocked with a Src kinase inhibitor.
Local changes in the lipid composition of TCR microclusters thus render the CD3ε cytoplasmic domain accessible during early stages of T cell activation.</pre>

</details>

<details><summary>Rank 8 · b832561b50eff3f4c7ab7aae4eef5f49 · document 33499189 · score 0.76433 · 223 tokens</summary>

<pre>Full activation of the T cell receptor requires both clustering and conformational changes at CD3.
T cell receptor (TCR-CD3) triggering involves both receptor clustering and conformational changes at the cytoplasmic tails of the CD3 subunits.
The mechanism by which TCRalphabeta ligand binding confers conformational changes to CD3 is unknown.
By using well-defined ligands, we showed that induction of the conformational change requires both multivalent engagement and the mobility restriction of the TCR-CD3 imposed by the plasma membrane.
The conformational change is elicited by cooperative rearrangements of two TCR-CD3 complexes and does not require accompanying changes in the structure of the TCRalphabeta ectodomains.
This conformational change at CD3 reverts upon ligand dissociation and is required for T cell activation.
Thus, our permissive geometry model provides a molecular mechanism that rationalizes how the information of ligand binding to TCRalphabeta is transmitted to the CD3 subunits and to the intracellular signaling machinery.</pre>

</details>

<details><summary>Rank 9 · 9e647799a1774d05a79db01fba1d8210 · document 9283422 · score 0.76105 · 249 tokens</summary>

<pre>T cell receptor-proximal signals are sustained in peripheral microclusters and terminated in the central supramolecular activation cluster.
T cell receptor (TCR) signaling is initiated and sustained in microclusters; however, it&#x27;s not known whether signaling also occurs in the TCR-rich central supramolecular activation cluster (cSMAC).
We showed that the cSMAC formed by fusion of microclusters contained more CD45 than microclusters and is a site enriched in lysobisphosphatidic acid, a lipid involved in sorting ubiquitinated membrane proteins for degradation.
Calcium signaling via TCR was blocked within 2 min by anti-MHCp treatment and 1 min by latrunculin-A treatment.
TCR-MHCp interactions in the cSMAC survived these perturbations for 10 min and hence were not sufficient to sustain signaling.
TCR microclusters were also resistant to disruption by anti-MHCp and latrunculin-A treatments.
We propose that TCR signaling is sustained by stabilized microclusters and is terminated in the cSMAC, a structure from which TCR are sorted for degradation.
Our studies reveal a role for F-actin in TCR signaling beyond microcluster formation.</pre>

</details>

<details><summary>Rank 10 · 33ad6a5c55080bf80179e493c596b77a · document 18834078 · score 0.75798 · 193 tokens</summary>

<pre>Secondary T cell–T cell synaptic interactions drive the differentiation of protective CD8+ T cells
Immunization results in the differentiation of CD8+ T cells, such that they acquire effector abilities and convert into a memory pool.
Priming of T cells takes place via an immunological synapse formed with an antigen-presenting cell (APC).
By disrupting synaptic stability at different times, we found that the differentiation of CD8+ T cells required cell interactions beyond those made with APCs.
We identified a critical differentiation period that required interactions between primed T cells.
We found that T cell–T cell synapses had a major role in the generation of protective CD8+ T cell memory.
T cell–T cell synapses allowed T cells to polarize critical secretion of interferon-γ (IFN-γ) toward each other.
Collective activation and homotypic clustering drove cytokine sharing and acted as regulatory stimuli for T cell differentiation.</pre>

Direct observation of ligand recognition by T cells

The activation of T cells through interaction of their T-cell receptors with antigenic peptide bound to major histocompatibility complex (MHC) on the surface of antigen presenting cells (APCs) is a crucial step in adaptive immunity.

Here we use three-dimensional fluorescence microscopy to visualize individual peptide–I-Ek class II MHC complexes labelled with the phycobiliprotein phycoerythrin in an effort to characterize T-cell sensitivity and the requirements for forming an immunological synapse in single cells.

T-cell-antigen recognition and the immunological synapse

Much excitement of the past five years in the area of T-cell-antigen recognition has centred around the immunological synapse — a complex cellular structure that forms at the interface of a T cell and a cell that expresses the appropriate peptide–MHC complexes.

Thanks to new imaging technologies, we are now beginning to understand the role of cell-surface molecules and some of their attendant signalling modules in the context of cell-to-cell communication.

Progress has been so rapid that T-cell-antigen recognition might be the first system in which the molecular basis of cell–cell recognition is understood.

The immunological synapse is a specialized cell-cell junction that is defined by large-scale spatial patterns of receptors and signaling molecules yet remains largely enigmatic in terms of formation and function.

We used supported bilayer membranes and nanometer-scale structures fabricated onto the underlying substrate to impose geometric constraints on immunological synapse formation.

Analysis of the resulting alternatively patterned synapses revealed a causal relation between the radial position of T cell receptors (TCRs) and signaling activity, with prolonged signaling from TCR microclusters that had been mechanically trapped in the peripheral regions of the synapse.

      &quot;tokens&quot;: 39,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;By using well-defined ligands, we showed that induction of the conformational change requires both multivalent engagement and the mobility restriction of the TCR-CD3 imposed by the plasma membrane.&quot;

<pre>{
  &quot;selected_units&quot;: [
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;faa189135b9f644503f4d9f61a5922a4&quot;,

      &quot;tokens&quot;: 33,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Recruitment of Nck by CD3ϵ Reveals a Ligand-Induced Conformational Change Essential for T Cell Receptor Signaling and Synapse Formation&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;a81b51ded29bbba5ad8273f15e5d67aa&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;b9479b9dcbdfb5236a5ff7cbe8d0f84b&quot;,

      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 788,
      &quot;end&quot;: 976,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 43,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Finally, by interfering with Nck-CD3 epsilon association in vivo, we demonstrate that TCR-CD3 recruitment of Nck is critical for maturation of the immune synapse and for T cell activation.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;80e4289afe10f1d482dd09a13cf7d5b1&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;8222881e245779d31fa4c7615e05cb3c&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;4422734&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 0,
      &quot;end&quot;: 51,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 9,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Direct observation of ligand recognition by T cells&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;5c0506e1b86c0b3d6e922268123c1d9c&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;8222881e245779d31fa4c7615e05cb3c&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;4422734&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 52,
      &quot;end&quot;: 284,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 46,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;The activation of T cells through interaction of their T-cell receptors with antigenic peptide bound to major histocompatibility complex (MHC) on the surface of antigen presenting cells (APCs) is a crucial step in adaptive immunity.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;5b716800158b635f9da3632ddf749318&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;8222881e245779d31fa4c7615e05cb3c&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;4422734&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 285,
      &quot;end&quot;: 570,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 55,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Here we use three-dimensional fluorescence microscopy to visualize individual peptide–I-Ek class II MHC complexes labelled with the phycobiliprotein phycoerythrin in an effort to characterize T-cell sensitivity and the requirements for forming an immunological synapse in single cells.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;45d0296e0416cb5ed2ac807267ed7b4d&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;8222881e245779d31fa4c7615e05cb3c&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;4422734&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 571,
      &quot;end&quot;: 885,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 63,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;We show that T cells expressing the CD4 antigen respond with transient calcium signalling to even a single agonist peptide–MHC ligand, and that the organization of molecules in the contact zone of the T cell and APC takes on the characteristics of an immunological synapse when only about ten agonists are present.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;9270e799eecbc56f54d31fb9f90e285a&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;8222881e245779d31fa4c7615e05cb3c&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;4422734&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 886,
      &quot;end&quot;: 1038,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 31,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;This sensitivity is highly dependant on CD4, because blocking this molecule with antibodies renders T cells unable to detect less than about 30 ligands.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;2e2970f4088b8fbedf7241625cb875ca&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;491f59498cad06f42087657a5fa9726f&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;5914739&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 0,
      &quot;end&quot;: 112,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 23,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Local changes in lipid environment of TCR microclusters regulate membrane binding by the CD3ε cytoplasmic domain&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;a38133b6f20450b1e0ebaf3b22561286&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;491f59498cad06f42087657a5fa9726f&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;5914739&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 1170,
      &quot;end&quot;: 1322,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 31,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Local changes in the lipid composition of TCR microclusters thus render the CD3ε cytoplasmic domain accessible during early stages of T cell activation.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;8c3981fe760d36c5cbe8a791a558b1c7&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;a67ce222cd70843cf45cb79234889e9c&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;15972906&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 0,
      &quot;end&quot;: 62,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 11,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Functional anatomy of T cell activation and synapse formation.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;14a4c6b944861c9557201a44eb5bbad3&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;a67ce222cd70843cf45cb79234889e9c&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;15972906&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 63,
      &quot;end&quot;: 154,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 15,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;T cell activation and function require a structured engagement of antigen-presenting cells.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;8607ae6f9bd10674bb529d5d2add4e07&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;a67ce222cd70843cf45cb79234889e9c&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;15972906&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 155,
      &quot;end&quot;: 388,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 39,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;These cell contacts are characterized by two distinct dynamics in vivo: transient contacts resulting from promigratory junctions called immunological kinapses or prolonged contacts from stable junctions called immunological synapses.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;eeefd0131606160a698ab27466a7dfc3&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;a67ce222cd70843cf45cb79234889e9c&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;15972906&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 389,
      &quot;end&quot;: 514,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 31,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Kinapses operate in the steady state to allow referencing to self-peptide-MHC (pMHC) and searching for pathogen-derived pMHC.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;8c682abedb681de27150963cc770d371&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;a67ce222cd70843cf45cb79234889e9c&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;15972906&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 515,
      &quot;end&quot;: 703,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 37,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Synapses are induced by T cell receptor (TCR) interactions with agonist pMHC under specific conditions and correlate with robust immune responses that generate effector and memory T cells.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;ad95b0b41885f424643eb673f76e6b1b&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;a67ce222cd70843cf45cb79234889e9c&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;15972906&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 704,
      &quot;end&quot;: 932,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 45,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;High-resolution imaging has revealed that the synapse is highly coordinated, integrating cell adhesion, TCR recognition of pMHC complexes, and an array of activating and inhibitory ligands to promote or prevent T cell signaling.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;a18507a615c423c7be94af3fc9774d47&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;a67ce222cd70843cf45cb79234889e9c&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;15972906&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 933,
      &quot;end&quot;: 1040,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 21,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;In this review, we examine the molecular components, geometry, and timing underlying kinapses and synapses.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;ec5aedfe7b94e7b77c65d04e8b97cb94&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;a67ce222cd70843cf45cb79234889e9c&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;15972906&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 1041,
      &quot;end&quot;: 1142,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 16,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;We integrate recent molecular and physiological data to provide a synthesis and suggest ways forward.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;8542d63c4f5764bf8eaee9e3c23a7b81&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;33ad6a5c55080bf80179e493c596b77a&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;18834078&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 234,
      &quot;end&quot;: 339,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 24,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Priming of T cells takes place via an immunological synapse formed with an antigen-presenting cell (APC).&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;21555e70d3f2879854be2c6a26cd7f9e&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;33ad6a5c55080bf80179e493c596b77a&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;18834078&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 598,
      &quot;end&quot;: 703,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 26,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;We found that T cell–T cell synapses had a major role in the generation of protective CD8+ T cell memory.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;1a990f4a32e90fc346184aa15e33e305&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;2303c32e96b778bf583b74fbd1b9d5f9&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;21746539&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 0,
      &quot;end&quot;: 56,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 12,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;T-cell-antigen recognition and the immunological synapse&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;bfefebd239ffb9817e7eec1928e0deff&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;2303c32e96b778bf583b74fbd1b9d5f9&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;21746539&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 57,
      &quot;end&quot;: 318,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 53,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Much excitement of the past five years in the area of T-cell-antigen recognition has centred around the immunological synapse — a complex cellular structure that forms at the interface of a T cell and a cell that expresses the appropriate peptide–MHC complexes.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;a0869493cfd1744b4b5105879bfdc190&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;2303c32e96b778bf583b74fbd1b9d5f9&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;21746539&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 319,
      &quot;end&quot;: 517,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 35,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Thanks to new imaging technologies, we are now beginning to understand the role of cell-surface molecules and some of their attendant signalling modules in the context of cell-to-cell communication.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;3f340ba9fdf0d3382c6cd7831fe4cf3b&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;2303c32e96b778bf583b74fbd1b9d5f9&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;21746539&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 518,
      &quot;end&quot;: 671,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 30,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Progress has been so rapid that T-cell-antigen recognition might be the first system in which the molecular basis of cell–cell recognition is understood.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;cfaaeb4da4ddc62d7ec0dff1a44b9afa&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;b832561b50eff3f4c7ab7aae4eef5f49&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;33499189&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,

      &quot;end&quot;: 98,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 19,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Full activation of the T cell receptor requires both clustering and conformational changes at CD3.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;403104384d16571047122dfb1fc727d7&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;b832561b50eff3f4c7ab7aae4eef5f49&quot;,

      &quot;end&quot;: 242,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 34,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;T cell receptor (TCR-CD3) triggering involves both receptor clustering and conformational changes at the cytoplasmic tails of the CD3 subunits.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;6d0d856eb9fc432d18ad5d053af40290&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;b832561b50eff3f4c7ab7aae4eef5f49&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;33499189&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 344,
      &quot;end&quot;: 541,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 39,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;By using well-defined ligands, we showed that induction of the conformational change requires both multivalent engagement and the mobility restriction of the TCR-CD3 imposed by the plasma membrane.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;76e12096b7bd0f264283bcd1855b6c7b&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;b832561b50eff3f4c7ab7aae4eef5f49&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;33499189&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 542,
      &quot;end&quot;: 726,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 41,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;The conformational change is elicited by cooperative rearrangements of two TCR-CD3 complexes and does not require accompanying changes in the structure of the TCRalphabeta ectodomains.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;5f8209591872d112305b3371af1896b3&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;732c3dbcb31d77a82edcf27b27f8d608&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;41982985&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 0,
      &quot;end&quot;: 76,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 16,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Altered TCR signaling from geometrically repatterned immunological synapses.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;90a7e2be6652cace67fd811af65d84c3&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;732c3dbcb31d77a82edcf27b27f8d608&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;41982985&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 77,
      &quot;end&quot;: 289,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 36,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;The immunological synapse is a specialized cell-cell junction that is defined by large-scale spatial patterns of receptors and signaling molecules yet remains largely enigmatic in terms of formation and function.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;1c45d9604080f6332e1ceb5f7dfac374&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;732c3dbcb31d77a82edcf27b27f8d608&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;41982985&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 290,
      &quot;end&quot;: 465,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 27,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;We used supported bilayer membranes and nanometer-scale structures fabricated onto the underlying substrate to impose geometric constraints on immunological synapse formation.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;7e8a94b5ce69f341ef437cb84c6e957c&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;732c3dbcb31d77a82edcf27b27f8d608&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;41982985&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 466,
      &quot;end&quot;: 755,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 51,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Analysis of the resulting alternatively patterned synapses revealed a causal relation between the radial position of T cell receptors (TCRs) and signaling activity, with prolonged signaling from TCR microclusters that had been mechanically trapped in the peripheral regions of the synapse.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;2b9318662dec5a60e798ff1a1b13d9c0&quot;,

      &quot;tokens&quot;: 28,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;These results are consistent with a model of the synapse in which spatial translocation of TCRs represents a direct mechanism of signal regulation.&quot;
    }

<pre>{
  &quot;selected_units&quot;: [
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;a81b51ded29bbba5ad8273f15e5d67aa&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;b9479b9dcbdfb5236a5ff7cbe8d0f84b&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;2714623&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 788,
      &quot;end&quot;: 976,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 43,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Finally, by interfering with Nck-CD3 epsilon association in vivo, we demonstrate that TCR-CD3 recruitment of Nck is critical for maturation of the immune synapse and for T cell activation.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;45d0296e0416cb5ed2ac807267ed7b4d&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;8222881e245779d31fa4c7615e05cb3c&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;4422734&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 571,
      &quot;end&quot;: 885,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 63,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;We show that T cells expressing the CD4 antigen respond with transient calcium signalling to even a single agonist peptide–MHC ligand, and that the organization of molecules in the contact zone of the T cell and APC takes on the characteristics of an immunological synapse when only about ten agonists are present.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;a38133b6f20450b1e0ebaf3b22561286&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;491f59498cad06f42087657a5fa9726f&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;5914739&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 1170,
      &quot;end&quot;: 1322,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 31,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Local changes in the lipid composition of TCR microclusters thus render the CD3ε cytoplasmic domain accessible during early stages of T cell activation.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;8c682abedb681de27150963cc770d371&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;a67ce222cd70843cf45cb79234889e9c&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;15972906&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 515,
      &quot;end&quot;: 703,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 37,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Synapses are induced by T cell receptor (TCR) interactions with agonist pMHC under specific conditions and correlate with robust immune responses that generate effector and memory T cells.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;ad95b0b41885f424643eb673f76e6b1b&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;a67ce222cd70843cf45cb79234889e9c&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;15972906&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 704,
      &quot;end&quot;: 932,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 45,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;High-resolution imaging has revealed that the synapse is highly coordinated, integrating cell adhesion, TCR recognition of pMHC complexes, and an array of activating and inhibitory ligands to promote or prevent T cell signaling.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;9a7a0c0550766773c2f3dda4cf00868f&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;42d84dabd5a8343f1479509b53552582&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;18758057&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 1074,
      &quot;end&quot;: 1256,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 61,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;The ligation of TCR/CD3 on CD4 or CD8 T cells led to CD3 nanoscale co-clustering or interaction with CD4 or CD8 co-receptors forming 200-500 nm nano-domains or &gt;500 nm micro-domains.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;8542d63c4f5764bf8eaee9e3c23a7b81&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;33ad6a5c55080bf80179e493c596b77a&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;18834078&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 234,
      &quot;end&quot;: 339,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 24,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Priming of T cells takes place via an immunological synapse formed with an antigen-presenting cell (APC).&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;7e8a94b5ce69f341ef437cb84c6e957c&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;732c3dbcb31d77a82edcf27b27f8d608&quot;,

      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 466,

      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Analysis of the resulting alternatively patterned synapses revealed a causal relation between the radial position of T cell receptors (TCRs) and signaling activity, with prolonged signaling from TCR microclusters that had been mechanically trapped in the peripheral regions of the synapse.&quot;

#### What V1 discarded / V2 recovered

<pre>{
  &quot;FIXED_SENTENCE_sentences_absent_in_V1&quot;: [
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;17e19ef38222d81a4cbe2fbb00b7da62&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;b9479b9dcbdfb5236a5ff7cbe8d0f84b&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;The T cell receptor complex (TCR-CD3) is composed of TCR alpha/beta ligand binding subunits bound to the CD3 subunits responsible for signal transduction.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;403104384d16571047122dfb1fc727d7&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;b832561b50eff3f4c7ab7aae4eef5f49&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;T cell receptor (TCR-CD3) triggering involves both receptor clustering and conformational changes at the cytoplasmic tails of the CD3 subunits.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;45d0296e0416cb5ed2ac807267ed7b4d&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;8222881e245779d31fa4c7615e05cb3c&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;We show that T cells expressing the CD4 antigen respond with transient calcium signalling to even a single agonist peptide–MHC ligand, and that the organization of molecules in the contact zone of the T cell and APC takes on the characteristics of an immunological synapse when only about ten agonists are present.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;6d0d856eb9fc432d18ad5d053af40290&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;b832561b50eff3f4c7ab7aae4eef5f49&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;By using well-defined ligands, we showed that induction of the conformational change requires both multivalent engagement and the mobility restriction of the TCR-CD3 imposed by the plasma membrane.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;76e12096b7bd0f264283bcd1855b6c7b&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;b832561b50eff3f4c7ab7aae4eef5f49&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;The conformational change is elicited by cooperative rearrangements of two TCR-CD3 complexes and does not require accompanying changes in the structure of the TCRalphabeta ectodomains.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;7e8a94b5ce69f341ef437cb84c6e957c&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;732c3dbcb31d77a82edcf27b27f8d608&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Analysis of the resulting alternatively patterned synapses revealed a causal relation between the radial position of T cell receptors (TCRs) and signaling activity, with prolonged signaling from TCR microclusters that had been mechanically trapped in the peripheral regions of the synapse.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;83c016ab7b06ab5a62bb94fe713e3a55&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;42d84dabd5a8343f1479509b53552582&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Direct molecular imaging of nano-spatial relationship between T cell receptor (TCR)/CD3 and CD4 or CD8 co-receptor before and after activation of a primary T cell has not been reported.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;9619e554c061906f9cd05b965807fc39&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;42d84dabd5a8343f1479509b53552582&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Importantly, CD28 co-stimulation remarkably enhanced TCR/CD3 nanoscale co-clustering or interaction with CD4 co-receptor within nano- or micro-domains on the membrane.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;9a7a0c0550766773c2f3dda4cf00868f&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;42d84dabd5a8343f1479509b53552582&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;The ligation of TCR/CD3 on CD4 or CD8 T cells led to CD3 nanoscale co-clustering or interaction with CD4 or CD8 co-receptors forming 200-500 nm nano-domains or &gt;500 nm micro-domains.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;a81b51ded29bbba5ad8273f15e5d67aa&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;b9479b9dcbdfb5236a5ff7cbe8d0f84b&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Finally, by interfering with Nck-CD3 epsilon association in vivo, we demonstrate that TCR-CD3 recruitment of Nck is critical for maturation of the immune synapse and for T cell activation.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;acb2c8a70a64c8b765f5d72baab5ce61&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;491f59498cad06f42087657a5fa9726f&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;The CD3ε and ζ cytoplasmic domains of the T cell receptor bind to the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane (PM), and a previous nuclear magnetic resonance structure showed that both tyrosines of the CD3ε immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activation motif partition into the bilayer.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;ad95b0b41885f424643eb673f76e6b1b&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;a67ce222cd70843cf45cb79234889e9c&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;High-resolution imaging has revealed that the synapse is highly coordinated, integrating cell adhesion, TCR recognition of pMHC complexes, and an array of activating and inhibitory ligands to promote or prevent T cell signaling.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;bfefebd239ffb9817e7eec1928e0deff&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;2303c32e96b778bf583b74fbd1b9d5f9&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Much excitement of the past five years in the area of T-cell-antigen recognition has centred around the immunological synapse — a complex cellular structure that forms at the interface of a T cell and a cell that expresses the appropriate peptide–MHC complexes.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;d273427e84ea8abc1950c26d358c304a&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;42d84dabd5a8343f1479509b53552582&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;NSOM/QD-Based Direct Visualization of CD3-Induced and CD28-Enhanced Nanospatial Coclustering of TCR and Coreceptor in Nanodomains in T Cell Activation&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;dc3f5648eac60d36199f1f4593b819d1&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;9e647799a1774d05a79db01fba1d8210&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;T cell receptor (TCR) signaling is initiated and sustained in microclusters; however, it&#x27;s not known whether signaling also occurs in the TCR-rich central supramolecular activation cluster (cSMAC).&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;ea15529278289dd21eb7a5319ce1b980&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;42d84dabd5a8343f1479509b53552582&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Such nano-spatial co-clustering of CD3 and CD4 or CD3 and CD8 appeared to be an intrinsic event of TCR/CD3 ligation, not purely limited to MHC engagement, and be driven by Lck phosphorylation.&quot;
    }
  ],
  &quot;QBGF_FULL_sentences_absent_in_V1&quot;: [
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;3f340ba9fdf0d3382c6cd7831fe4cf3b&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;2303c32e96b778bf583b74fbd1b9d5f9&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Progress has been so rapid that T-cell-antigen recognition might be the first system in which the molecular basis of cell–cell recognition is understood.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;403104384d16571047122dfb1fc727d7&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;b832561b50eff3f4c7ab7aae4eef5f49&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;T cell receptor (TCR-CD3) triggering involves both receptor clustering and conformational changes at the cytoplasmic tails of the CD3 subunits.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;45d0296e0416cb5ed2ac807267ed7b4d&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;8222881e245779d31fa4c7615e05cb3c&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;We show that T cells expressing the CD4 antigen respond with transient calcium signalling to even a single agonist peptide–MHC ligand, and that the organization of molecules in the contact zone of the T cell and APC takes on the characteristics of an immunological synapse when only about ten agonists are present.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;5b716800158b635f9da3632ddf749318&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;8222881e245779d31fa4c7615e05cb3c&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Here we use three-dimensional fluorescence microscopy to visualize individual peptide–I-Ek class II MHC complexes labelled with the phycobiliprotein phycoerythrin in an effort to characterize T-cell sensitivity and the requirements for forming an immunological synapse in single cells.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;5c0506e1b86c0b3d6e922268123c1d9c&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;8222881e245779d31fa4c7615e05cb3c&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;The activation of T cells through interaction of their T-cell receptors with antigenic peptide bound to major histocompatibility complex (MHC) on the surface of antigen presenting cells (APCs) is a crucial step in adaptive immunity.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;6d0d856eb9fc432d18ad5d053af40290&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;b832561b50eff3f4c7ab7aae4eef5f49&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;By using well-defined ligands, we showed that induction of the conformational change requires both multivalent engagement and the mobility restriction of the TCR-CD3 imposed by the plasma membrane.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;76e12096b7bd0f264283bcd1855b6c7b&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;b832561b50eff3f4c7ab7aae4eef5f49&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;The conformational change is elicited by cooperative rearrangements of two TCR-CD3 complexes and does not require accompanying changes in the structure of the TCRalphabeta ectodomains.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;7e8a94b5ce69f341ef437cb84c6e957c&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;732c3dbcb31d77a82edcf27b27f8d608&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Analysis of the resulting alternatively patterned synapses revealed a causal relation between the radial position of T cell receptors (TCRs) and signaling activity, with prolonged signaling from TCR microclusters that had been mechanically trapped in the peripheral regions of the synapse.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;8607ae6f9bd10674bb529d5d2add4e07&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;a67ce222cd70843cf45cb79234889e9c&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;These cell contacts are characterized by two distinct dynamics in vivo: transient contacts resulting from promigratory junctions called immunological kinapses or prolonged contacts from stable junctions called immunological synapses.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;90a7e2be6652cace67fd811af65d84c3&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;732c3dbcb31d77a82edcf27b27f8d608&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;The immunological synapse is a specialized cell-cell junction that is defined by large-scale spatial patterns of receptors and signaling molecules yet remains largely enigmatic in terms of formation and function.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;9270e799eecbc56f54d31fb9f90e285a&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;8222881e245779d31fa4c7615e05cb3c&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;This sensitivity is highly dependant on CD4, because blocking this molecule with antibodies renders T cells unable to detect less than about 30 ligands.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;a0869493cfd1744b4b5105879bfdc190&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;2303c32e96b778bf583b74fbd1b9d5f9&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Thanks to new imaging technologies, we are now beginning to understand the role of cell-surface molecules and some of their attendant signalling modules in the context of cell-to-cell communication.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;a81b51ded29bbba5ad8273f15e5d67aa&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;b9479b9dcbdfb5236a5ff7cbe8d0f84b&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Finally, by interfering with Nck-CD3 epsilon association in vivo, we demonstrate that TCR-CD3 recruitment of Nck is critical for maturation of the immune synapse and for T cell activation.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;ad95b0b41885f424643eb673f76e6b1b&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;a67ce222cd70843cf45cb79234889e9c&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;High-resolution imaging has revealed that the synapse is highly coordinated, integrating cell adhesion, TCR recognition of pMHC complexes, and an array of activating and inhibitory ligands to promote or prevent T cell signaling.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;bfefebd239ffb9817e7eec1928e0deff&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;2303c32e96b778bf583b74fbd1b9d5f9&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Much excitement of the past five years in the area of T-cell-antigen recognition has centred around the immunological synapse — a complex cellular structure that forms at the interface of a T cell and a cell that expresses the appropriate peptide–MHC complexes.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;eeefd0131606160a698ab27466a7dfc3&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;a67ce222cd70843cf45cb79234889e9c&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Kinapses operate in the steady state to allow referencing to self-peptide-MHC (pMHC) and searching for pathogen-derived pMHC.&quot;
    }
  ],

<details><summary>Rank 1 · 7924d7e557b1bce8a2b7ae768c5ac6e3 · document 544971 · score 0.79999 · 198 tokens</summary>

<pre>DNA Deamination Mediates Innate Immunity to Retroviral Infection
CEM15/APOBEC3G is a cellular protein required for resistance to infection by virion infectivity factor (Vif)-deficient human immunodeficiency virus (HIV).
Here, using a murine leukemia virus (MLV)-based system, we provide evidence that CEM15/APOBEC3G is a DNA deaminase that is incorporated into virions during viral production and subsequently triggers massive deamination of deoxycytidine to deoxyuridine within the retroviral minus (first)-strand cDNA, thus providing a probable trigger for viral destruction.
Furthermore, HIV Vif can protect MLV from this CEM15/APOBEC3G-dependent restriction.
These findings imply that targeted DNA deamination is a major strategy of innate immunity to retroviruses and likely also contributes to the sequence variation observed in many viruses (including HIV).</pre>

</details>

<details><summary>Rank 2 · 4f8866f77f2ce5fa4f64b9bc35ec4f17 · document 2638387 · score 0.79513 · 299 tokens</summary>

<pre>The cytidine deaminase CEM15 induces hypermutation in newly synthesized HIV-1 DNA
High mutation frequency during reverse transcription has a principal role in the genetic variation of primate lentiviral populations.
It is the main driving force for the generation of drug resistance and the escape from immune surveillance.
G to A hypermutation is one of the characteristics of primate lentiviruses, as well as other retroviruses, during replication in vivo and in cell culture.
The molecular mechanisms of this process, however, remain to be clarified.
Here, we demonstrate that CEM15 (also known as apolipoprotein B mRNA editing enzyme, catalytic polypeptide-like 3G; APOBEC3G), an endogenous inhibitor of human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) replication, is a cytidine deaminase and is able to induce G to A hypermutation in newly synthesized viral DNA.
This effect can be counteracted by the HIV-1 virion infectivity factor (Vif).
It seems that this viral DNA mutator is a viral defence mechanism in host cells that may induce either lethal hypermutation or instability of the incoming nascent viral reverse transcripts, which could account for the Vif-defective phenotype.
Importantly, the accumulation of CEM15-mediated non-lethal hypermutation in the replicating viral genome could potently contribute to the genetic variation of primate lentiviral populations.</pre>

</details>

<details><summary>Rank 3 · 13b3c656f6b3a4cc17211a1f326805ce · document 4347374 · score 0.71907 · 319 tokens</summary>

<pre>Broad antiretroviral defence by human APOBEC3G through lethal editing of nascent reverse transcripts
Viral replication usually requires that innate intracellular lines of defence be overcome, a task usually accomplished by specialized viral gene products.
The virion infectivity factor (Vif) protein of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) is required during the late stages of viral production to counter the antiviral activity of APOBEC3G (apolipoprotein B mRNA-editing enzyme, catalytic polypeptide-like 3G; also known as CEM15), a protein expressed notably in human T lymphocytes.
When produced in the presence of APOBEC3G, vif-defective virus is non-infectious.
APOBEC3G is closely related to APOBEC1, the central component of an RNA-editing complex that deaminates a cytosine residue in apoB messenger RNA.
APOBEC family members also have potent DNA mutator activity through dC deamination; however, whether the editing potential of APOBEC3G has any relevance to HIV inhibition is unknown.
Here, we demonstrate that it does, as APOBEC3G exerts its antiviral effect during reverse transcription to trigger G-to-A hypermutation in the nascent retroviral DNA.
We also find that APOBEC3G can act on a broad range of retroviruses in addition to HIV, suggesting that hypermutation by editing is a general innate defence mechanism against this important group of pathogens.</pre>

</details>

<details><summary>Rank 4 · d12e34f6ba96632f40ce380cf510784c · document 22703082 · score 0.70725 · 214 tokens</summary>

<pre>Helicobacter pylori infection triggers aberrant expression of activation-induced cytidine deaminase in gastric epithelium
Infection with Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) is a risk factor for the development of gastric cancer.
Here we show that infection of gastric epithelial cells with &#x27;cag&#x27; pathogenicity island (cagPAI)-positive H. pylori induced aberrant expression of activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID), a member of the cytidine-deaminase family that acts as a DNA- and RNA-editing enzyme, via the IκB kinase–dependent nuclear factor-κB activation pathway.
H. pylori–mediated upregulation of AID resulted in the accumulation of nucleotide alterations in the TP53 tumor suppressor gene in gastric cells in vitro.
Our findings provide evidence that aberrant AID expression caused by H. pylori infection might be a mechanism of mutation accumulation in the gastric mucosa during H. pylori–associated gastric carcinogenesis.</pre>

</details>

<details><summary>Rank 5 · 035e9a9d982eea1627319f924048f16a · document 12871002 · score 0.70477 · 263 tokens</summary>

<pre>CDE-1 Affects Chromosome Segregation through Uridylation of CSR-1-Bound siRNAs
We have studied the function of a conserved germline-specific nucleotidyltransferase protein, CDE-1, in RNAi and chromosome segregation in C. elegans.
CDE-1 localizes specifically to mitotic chromosomes in embryos.
This localization requires the RdRP EGO-1, which physically interacts with CDE-1, and the Argonaute protein CSR-1.
We found that CDE-1 is required for the uridylation of CSR-1 bound siRNAs, and that in the absence of CDE-1 these siRNAs accumulate to inappropriate levels, accompanied by defects in both meiotic and mitotic chromosome segregation.
Elevated siRNA levels are associated with erroneous gene silencing, most likely through the inappropriate loading of CSR-1 siRNAs into other Argonaute proteins.
We propose a model in which CDE-1 restricts specific EGO-1-generated siRNAs to the CSR-1 mediated, chromosome associated RNAi pathway, thus separating it from other endogenous RNAi pathways.
The conserved nature of CDE-1 suggests that similar sorting mechanisms may operate in other animals, including mammals.</pre>

</details>

<details><summary>Rank 6 · 9873f81660fe595d8bc483f20a35c28e · document 7029990 · score 0.69688 · 250 tokens</summary>

<pre>Stress-induced apoptosis associated with null mutation of ADAR1 RNA editing deaminase gene.
One type of RNA editing involves the conversion of adenosine residues into inosine in double-stranded RNA through the action of adenosine deaminases acting on RNA (ADAR).
A-to-I RNA editing of the coding sequence could result in synthesis of proteins not directly encoded in the genome.
ADAR edits also non-coding sequences of target RNAs, such as introns and 3&#x27;-untranslated regions, which may affect splicing, translation, and mRNA stability.
Three mammalian ADAR gene family members (ADAR1-3) have been identified.
Here we investigated phenotypes of mice homozygous for ADAR1 null mutation.
Although live ADAR1-/- embryos with normal gross appearance could be recovered up to E11.5, widespread apoptosis was detected in many tissues.
Fibroblasts derived from ADAR1-/- embryos were also prone to apoptosis induced by serum deprivation.
Our results demonstrate an essential requirement for ADAR1 in embryogenesis and suggest that it functions to promote survival of numerous tissues by editing one or more double-stranded RNAs required for protection against stress-induced apoptosis.</pre>

</details>

<details><summary>Rank 7 · 0ef3b81678d17ebf6798372124f2760a · document 1569031 · score 0.68955 · 287 tokens</summary>

<pre>RNase H and Postreplication Repair Protect Cells from Ribonucleotides Incorporated in DNA
The chemical identity and integrity of the genome is challenged by the incorporation of ribonucleoside triphosphates (rNTPs) in place of deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates (dNTPs) during replication.
Misincorporation is limited by the selectivity of DNA replicases.
We show that accumulation of ribonucleoside monophosphates (rNMPs) in the genome causes replication stress and has toxic consequences, particularly in the absence of RNase H1 and RNase H2, which remove rNMPs.
We demonstrate that postreplication repair (PRR) pathways-MMS2-dependent template switch and Pol ζ-dependent bypass-are crucial for tolerating the presence of rNMPs in the chromosomes; indeed, we show that Pol ζ efficiently replicates over 1-4 rNMPs.
Moreover, cells lacking RNase H accumulate mono- and polyubiquitylated PCNA and have a constitutively activated PRR.
Our findings describe a crucial function for RNase H1, RNase H2, template switch, and translesion DNA synthesis in overcoming rNTPs misincorporated during DNA replication, and may be relevant for the pathogenesis of Aicardi-Goutières syndrome.</pre>

</details>

<details><summary>Rank 8 · eba2aca493badcd22c9f9a03af029af1 · document 5633957 · score 0.68650 · 360 tokens</summary>

<pre>Degradation of Cellular miR-27 by a Novel, Highly Abundant Viral Transcript Is Important for Efficient Virus Replication In Vivo
Cytomegaloviruses express large amounts of viral miRNAs during lytic infection, yet, they only modestly alter the cellular miRNA profile.
The most prominent alteration upon lytic murine cytomegalovirus (MCMV) infection is the rapid degradation of the cellular miR-27a and miR-27b.
Here, we report that this regulation is mediated by the ∼1.7 kb spliced and highly abundant MCMV m169 transcript.
Specificity to miR-27a/b is mediated by a single, apparently optimized, miRNA binding site located in its 3&#x27;-UTR.
This site is easily and efficiently retargeted to other cellular and viral miRNAs by target site replacement.
Expression of the 3&#x27;-UTR of m169 by an adenoviral vector was sufficient to mediate its function, indicating that no other viral factors are essential in this process.
Degradation of miR-27a/b was found to be accompanied by 3&#x27;-tailing and -trimming.
Despite its dramatic effect on miRNA stability, we found this interaction to be mutual, indicating potential regulation of m169 by miR-27a/b.
Most interestingly, three mutant viruses no longer able to target miR-27a/b, either due to miRNA target site disruption or target site replacement, showed significant attenuation in multiple organs as early as 4 days post infection, indicating that degradation of miR-27a/b is important for efficient MCMV replication in vivo.</pre>

<details><summary>Rank 9 · 95f0c8aa96ad38bacb26e6503b6fa799 · document 31407112 · score 0.68606 · 270 tokens</summary>

<pre>Deficiency in l-serine deaminase results in abnormal growth and cell division of Escherichia coli K-12.
The loss of the ability to deaminate l-serine severely impairs growth and cell division in Escherichia coli K-12.
A strain from which the three genes (sdaA, sdaB, tdcG) coding for this organism&#x27;s three l-serine deaminases had been deleted grows well in glucose minimal medium but, on subculture into minimal medium with glucose and casamino acids, it makes very large, abnormally shaped cells, many of which lyse.
When inoculated into Luria-Bertani (LB) broth with or without glucose, it makes very long filaments.
Provision of S-adenosylmethionine restores cell division in LB broth with glucose, and repairs much of the difficulty in growth in medium with casamino acids.
We suggest that replication of E. coli is regulated by methylation, that an unusually high intracellular l-serine concentration, in the presence of other amino acids, starves the cell for S-adenosylmethionine and that it is the absence of S-adenosylmethionine and/or of C1-tetrahydrofolate derivatives that prevents normal cell division.</pre>

<pre>Analysis of human cytomegalovirus-encoded microRNA activity during infection.
MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are expressed in a wide variety of organisms, ranging from plants to animals, and are key posttranscriptional regulators of gene expression.
Virally encoded miRNAs are unique in that they could potentially target both viral and host genes.
Indeed, we have previously demonstrated that a human cytomegalovirus (HCMV)-encoded miRNA, miR-UL112, downregulates the expression of a host immune gene, MICB.
Remarkably, it was shown that the same miRNA also downregulates immediate-early viral genes and that its ectopic expression resulted in reduced viral replication and viral titers.
The targets for most of the viral miRNAs, and hence their functions, are still unknown.

Thus, we suggest that in addition to miR-UL112, two additional HCMV miRNAs control the life cycle of the virus.</pre>

      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;These findings imply that targeted DNA deamination is a major strategy of innate immunity to retroviruses and likely also contributes to the sequence variation observed in many viruses (including HIV).&quot;

    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;3e5ecf5d48a5778bd435e4cd3993682c&quot;,

      &quot;end&quot;: 288,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 52,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;The chemical identity and integrity of the genome is challenged by the incorporation of ribonucleoside triphosphates (rNTPs) in place of deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates (dNTPs) during replication.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;60de78348468d4e098c1bb92e09bbe46&quot;,

      &quot;start&quot;: 355,
      &quot;end&quot;: 563,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 53,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;We show that accumulation of ribonucleoside monophosphates (rNMPs) in the genome causes replication stress and has toxic consequences, particularly in the absence of RNase H1 and RNase H2, which remove rNMPs.&quot;

      &quot;end&quot;: 1175,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 57,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Our findings describe a crucial function for RNase H1, RNase H2, template switch, and translesion DNA synthesis in overcoming rNTPs misincorporated during DNA replication, and may be relevant for the pathogenesis of Aicardi-Goutières syndrome.&quot;

      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Here, we demonstrate that CEM15 (also known as apolipoprotein B mRNA editing enzyme, catalytic polypeptide-like 3G; APOBEC3G), an endogenous inhibitor of human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) replication, is a cytidine deaminase and is able to induce G to A hypermutation in newly synthesized viral DNA.&quot;

<pre>{

      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;DNA Deamination Mediates Innate Immunity to Retroviral Infection&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;7afe3bc0f5d8e21255eae2396fd367fb&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;7924d7e557b1bce8a2b7ae768c5ac6e3&quot;,

      &quot;end&quot;: 219,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 40,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;CEM15/APOBEC3G is a cellular protein required for resistance to infection by virion infectivity factor (Vif)-deficient human immunodeficiency virus (HIV).&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;973f28d3f815f8954587baecfb8096d3&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;7924d7e557b1bce8a2b7ae768c5ac6e3&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;544971&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 220,
      &quot;end&quot;: 577,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 83,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Here, using a murine leukemia virus (MLV)-based system, we provide evidence that CEM15/APOBEC3G is a DNA deaminase that is incorporated into virions during viral production and subsequently triggers massive deamination of deoxycytidine to deoxyuridine within the retroviral minus (first)-strand cDNA, thus providing a probable trigger for viral destruction.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;c9c24d6b1aa20084d3d33befe506ea9e&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;7924d7e557b1bce8a2b7ae768c5ac6e3&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;544971&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 578,
      &quot;end&quot;: 662,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 24,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Furthermore, HIV Vif can protect MLV from this CEM15/APOBEC3G-dependent restriction.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;9bae72e21e26e269ce0164a9fd9c5c7e&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;7924d7e557b1bce8a2b7ae768c5ac6e3&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;544971&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 663,
      &quot;end&quot;: 864,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 35,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;These findings imply that targeted DNA deamination is a major strategy of innate immunity to retroviruses and likely also contributes to the sequence variation observed in many viruses (including HIV).&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;3e5ecf5d48a5778bd435e4cd3993682c&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;0ef3b81678d17ebf6798372124f2760a&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;1569031&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 90,
      &quot;end&quot;: 288,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 52,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;The chemical identity and integrity of the genome is challenged by the incorporation of ribonucleoside triphosphates (rNTPs) in place of deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates (dNTPs) during replication.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;4f8866f77f2ce5fa4f64b9bc35ec4f17&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;4f8866f77f2ce5fa4f64b9bc35ec4f17&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;2638387&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;PASSAGE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 0,
      &quot;end&quot;: 1375,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 299,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;The cytidine deaminase CEM15 induces hypermutation in newly synthesized HIV-1 DNA\nHigh mutation frequency during reverse transcription has a principal role in the genetic variation of primate lentiviral populations.\nIt is the main driving force for the generation of drug resistance and the escape from immune surveillance.\nG to A hypermutation is one of the characteristics of primate lentiviruses, as well as other retroviruses, during replication in vivo and in cell culture.\nThe molecular mechanisms of this process, however, remain to be clarified.\nHere, we demonstrate that CEM15 (also known as apolipoprotein B mRNA editing enzyme, catalytic polypeptide-like 3G; APOBEC3G), an endogenous inhibitor of human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) replication, is a cytidine deaminase and is able to induce G to A hypermutation in newly synthesized viral DNA.\nThis effect can be counteracted by the HIV-1 virion infectivity factor (Vif).\nIt seems that this viral DNA mutator is a viral defence mechanism in host cells that may induce either lethal hypermutation or instability of the incoming nascent viral reverse transcripts, which could account for the Vif-defective phenotype.\nImportantly, the accumulation of CEM15-mediated non-lethal hypermutation in the replicating viral genome could potently contribute to the genetic variation of primate lentiviral populations.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;d2a2b42f20e278c3df32a54d3892c0b2&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;13b3c656f6b3a4cc17211a1f326805ce&quot;,
      &quot;document&quot;: &quot;4347374&quot;,
      &quot;kind&quot;: &quot;SENTENCE&quot;,
      &quot;start&quot;: 811,
      &quot;end&quot;: 993,
      &quot;tokens&quot;: 40,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;APOBEC family members also have potent DNA mutator activity through dC deamination; however, whether the editing potential of APOBEC3G has any relevance to HIV inhibition is unknown.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;99d319a2931efeeb92483ba1089996f5&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;13b3c656f6b3a4cc17211a1f326805ce&quot;,

      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;A strain from which the three genes (sdaA, sdaB, tdcG) coding for this organism&#x27;s three l-serine deaminases had been deleted grows well in glucose minimal medium but, on subculture into minimal medium with glucose and casamino acids, it makes very large, abnormally shaped cells, many of which lyse.&quot;

      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Here, we demonstrate that CEM15 (also known as apolipoprotein B mRNA editing enzyme, catalytic polypeptide-like 3G; APOBEC3G), an endogenous inhibitor of human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) replication, is a cytidine deaminase and is able to induce G to A hypermutation in newly synthesized viral DNA.&quot;

    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;35d7ffd5ae4530408524ef52ea4479ee&quot;,

      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;We found that CDE-1 is required for the uridylation of CSR-1 bound siRNAs, and that in the absence of CDE-1 these siRNAs accumulate to inappropriate levels, accompanied by defects in both meiotic and mitotic chromosome segregation.&quot;

      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;0ef3b81678d17ebf6798372124f2760a&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;The chemical identity and integrity of the genome is challenged by the incorporation of ribonucleoside triphosphates (rNTPs) in place of deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates (dNTPs) during replication.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;560d62dedafc35675aff77eb51e47ad1&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;13b3c656f6b3a4cc17211a1f326805ce&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;APOBEC3G is closely related to APOBEC1, the central component of an RNA-editing complex that deaminates a cytosine residue in apoB messenger RNA.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;60de78348468d4e098c1bb92e09bbe46&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;0ef3b81678d17ebf6798372124f2760a&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;We show that accumulation of ribonucleoside monophosphates (rNMPs) in the genome causes replication stress and has toxic consequences, particularly in the absence of RNase H1 and RNase H2, which remove rNMPs.&quot;

    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;63cc04dff445986bbc397cff75389a2b&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;9873f81660fe595d8bc483f20a35c28e&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;One type of RNA editing involves the conversion of adenosine residues into inosine in double-stranded RNA through the action of adenosine deaminases acting on RNA (ADAR).&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;6b9851742b5bea3c79019c23cbaae5f1&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;eba2aca493badcd22c9f9a03af029af1&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Most interestingly, three mutant viruses no longer able to target miR-27a/b, either due to miRNA target site disruption or target site replacement, showed significant attenuation in multiple organs as early as 4 days post infection, indicating that degradation of miR-27a/b is important for efficient MCMV replication in vivo.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;6cf226d68d2594d281b8c3303e2b3cec&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;4f8866f77f2ce5fa4f64b9bc35ec4f17&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;It seems that this viral DNA mutator is a viral defence mechanism in host cells that may induce either lethal hypermutation or instability of the incoming nascent viral reverse transcripts, which could account for the Vif-defective phenotype.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;973f28d3f815f8954587baecfb8096d3&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;7924d7e557b1bce8a2b7ae768c5ac6e3&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Here, using a murine leukemia virus (MLV)-based system, we provide evidence that CEM15/APOBEC3G is a DNA deaminase that is incorporated into virions during viral production and subsequently triggers massive deamination of deoxycytidine to deoxyuridine within the retroviral minus (first)-strand cDNA, thus providing a probable trigger for viral destruction.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;99d319a2931efeeb92483ba1089996f5&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;13b3c656f6b3a4cc17211a1f326805ce&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Here, we demonstrate that it does, as APOBEC3G exerts its antiviral effect during reverse transcription to trigger G-to-A hypermutation in the nascent retroviral DNA.&quot;
    },
    {
      &quot;unit_id&quot;: &quot;9bae72e21e26e269ce0164a9fd9c5c7e&quot;,
      &quot;parent&quot;: &quot;7924d7e557b1bce8a2b7ae768c5ac6e3&quot;,
      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;These findings imply that targeted DNA deamination is a major strategy of innate immunity to retroviruses and likely also contributes to the sequence variation observed in many viruses (including HIV).&quot;
    },

      &quot;text&quot;: &quot;Our findings describe a crucial function for RNase H1, RNase H2, template switch, and translesion DNA synthesis in overcoming rNTPs misincorporated during DNA replication, and may be relevant for the pathogenesis of Aicardi-Goutières syndrome.&quot;
